speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. Brooks (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
maintopic: STATEMENT AS TO EFFECT OF HOSPITAL PLAN ON TREATMENT OF VETERANS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 20 the hon. member for York-Sunbury asked me the following question:
Can the minister inform this house of the effect the forthcoming provincial hospital insurance plans may have on the hospitalization and treatment of veterans and upon the operation of hospitals administered by his department?
I took the question as notice and now wish to make the following reply. My department has been greatly interested in the effect which the development of provincial hospital insurance plans might have upon the hospitalization and treatment of veterans and upon the operation of departmental hospitals. Officials of my department have been working closely with officials of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the provinces in this connection.
It is my intention that the operation of provincial hospital insurance plans will in no way adversely affect the rights and privileges of treatment which any veteran now enjoys at the hands of the department. Departmental hospitals located in those provinces participating in the federal-provincial arrangements for hospital insurance will be recognized by the province for the provision of insured services to veterans. This means that many of the services now provided, to veteran patients at the expense of the department or of the veteran himself will in future be provided in departmental hospitals at the expense of the hospital insurance plan. It does not mean that the services of the hospital will be extended beyond the present limits to citizens of the province who are non-veterans, or that the services provided to veteran patients will be in any way diminished.
It is a feature of all provincial hospital insurance plans that every resident of the province will be entitled to necessary hospitalization under the plan. Even so, the hospitalization and treatment of pensionable war-connected disabilities will remain the responsibility of the department alone. Such treatment will continue to be provided in departmental hospitals or elsewhere at the expense of the department and will not be charged against the provincial plan.
The veteran who is in receipt of war veterans' allowance and who is a resident of a participating province is entitled to hospitalization under the insurance plan on the same basis as other residents of the province. However, long usage and custom have firmly

Inquiries of the Ministry established the concept that the department has a responsibility under certain conditions for the hospitalization and treatment of this class of veteran. It is not the intention of the department to deny this responsibility. Therefore arrangements have been made by the department to pay, on behalf of the war veterans allowance recipient, any premium necessary to have him insured under the plan. Once the veteran war veterans allowance recipient is thus protected by the insurance plan, hospitalization in departmental hospitals or elsewhere will be at the expense of the plan. Co-insurance charges, where these are in effect, and medical and surgical costs will be at the expense of the department.
All other veterans who are residents of a province having a provincial hospital insurance plan will be covered by the plan as residents of the province. They will have the privilege of admission to departmental hospitals located in their province on a beds available basis, and the cost of this hospitalization will be recovered from the plan. The demand for other general hospital beds in the province will be lessened by the number of veterans who are thus admitted to departmental hospitals.
The existing regulations governing the hospitalization and treatment of veterans will be retained in their present form for the benefit of those veterans who are residents of nonparticipating provinces and for those veterans who, for one reason or another, are not covered by a provincial plan. Suitable provisions will be made to deal with those veterans whose hospitalization will henceforth be a charge against the provincial plan.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday afternoon, after pointing out that the constituency of Bellechasse partakes structurally of the three physiographic regions which characterize the area in which it is comprised, I gave a brief description of the first of these regions, referred to as the St. Lawrence plain, calling the attention of the Ministers of Public Works and of Transport to the urgency of certain undertakings.
Beyond this St. Lawrence plain, and again in a southerly direction, we find the central plateau whose mean altitude, over a distance of 20 miles is between 1,000 and 2,000 feet, the highest point in the area being the St. Magloire bonnet, which has an altitude of 2,700 feet. The surface of that second area is not as flat as the first and gives the general impression of being a rolling plateau. The soil is rocky, difficult to work, and its productivity is relatively low.
Finally, in the extreme southern area, beyond the Buckland and St. Philemon crests, the ground flattens once more to form a large plain. This is called the St. Jean ramp, after the river towards which it slopes. The soil there is better, not as rocky as on the central plateau, and more suited to large scale farming.
In any event, in these latter two regions, the farmer is not always able to live by farming alone. In the winter time a number of them must work in the bush and cut wood for sale to companies. Others operate woodlots on their own land, as on nearly half

the other farms in the province. According to recent statistics prepared by the Catholic Farmers' Union, out of 134,336 farms in the province of Quebec, there are 63,546 whose occupants have to supplement their agricultural revenue with outside work, to a varying degree. To a large extent this supplementary income is provided by the operation of woodlots on the farms themselves.
The pulp and paper industry is one of the foremost resources of the province of Quebec. Indeed, statistics show that, for the years 1948 to 1951, the average consumption of pulpwood was 5,206,000 cords annually. Now then, though the greater part of it comes from land owned by the companies or from the working of crown lands, none the less an average of 700,000 cords annually during the same period, came from farm woodlots, representing 13 per cent of the whole supply. This gives us an idea of the importance to the farmer of the province of Quebec of the pulp and paper industry.
Unfortunately, it must be said that the treatment the farmer receives from the companies which buy his wood is by no means always in accordance with the standards of equity and justice. On the basis of rather detailed studies, the Catholic Farmer's Union maintains that unless he receives at least $20 a cord for pulpwood, the farmer cannot cover his costs taking into account his labour and a small interest on the capital represented by his farm. In 1955, prices paid the settlers and farmers varied between $10 and $17 a cord. Even this year the price being lower than production costs, selling is slow because of the considerable supplies which the companies took care to pile up. Unfortunately, there are at present thousands of cords of pulpwood from farm woodlots along the roads of the constituency of Bellechasse.
The situation is all the more serious because, when they buy, paper companies wait for the right time, for instance in late spring, when the farmer has no choice but to sell, so as to have a little cash to pay his taxes and buy fertilizer or seed. So, while timber cut on crown lands costs the companies upwards of $30 a cord by the time it reaches their mills, they manage to reduce to a third of that sum the price they pay to the farmer.
The report just issued by the Restrictive Trade Practices Commission constitutes an appalling indictment. It shows that certain companies deliberately and systematically
The Address-Mr. Dorion resorted to illegal and objectionable practices in purchasing pulpwood from settlers and farmers, and did so in accordance with a concerted plan, in a clearly unfair and inhuman fashion.
Such procedures should not be tolerated any longer. If I remember well, the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. Fulton) has, in any case, informed the public that this report was under consideration and that he had the firm intention of taking action if the facts established did come under the provisions of the Combines Investigation Act. I commend him warmly on it, and I may add that repressive measures would be insufficient to correct the situation.
Like some other provinces, two years ago the government of Quebec passed an act called the agricultural produce act. It is, in a way, a transposition of the industrial relations act on the agricultural level. According to this law the producers of each area may form associations, enter into agreement with the buyers of their products and establish yearly terms for their marketing. Dairy farmers, maple and pulpwood producers are now developing this system. The fact remains that sales depend on the market demand and that prices may vary from one area to the other, or even from province to province. I am asking the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) if it would not be possible to submit this issue to the federal price stabilization board. By combining the advantages of the provincial and federal acts, we may succeed in helping in a large way that significant group of rural people who have woodlots on their farms. At the same time, we would stress the basic fact, which has but too often been ignored by our opponents, that understanding and harmony are best promoted and the greatest progress is made in the interest of national unity when the federal government and the provinces have a mutual regard for their respective laws and powers.
Once engaged in this direction, the federal government could also encourage our farmers to protect their woodlots and to practice forestry. We have in Quebec technicians trained in our forestry school upon whom the government could draw in order to help create experimental farms for the main purpose of preserving and developing our forests. The southern part of the constituency of Bellechasse would welcome such an undertaking. Our young people would be more inclined to resist the attraction of the cities and would find happiness and prosperity on the farms.

The Address-Mr. Dorion The speech from the throne expresses the government's intention to establish a small business agency. Such an initiative is the more welcome since it can still be of great advantage to our rural population. In the past, handicrafts, in a great variety of forms, were flourishing in the rural areas. They have been almost wholly eliminated by mechanical progress, concentration of capital, and the establishment of joint-stock companies in the larger centres. Nevertheless, there is still room, particularly in our rural areas, for the establishment and development of small businesses. In Bellechasse, we have a few small concerns using hardwood for the manufacture of furniture and kitchen utensils.
The relations between employer and employees are such as to guarantee social peace. There, people are still devoted to craftsmanship, so admirably sung by Peguy, and to that art of workmanship which is as an extension and most concrete expression of human personality.
Those small businesses are very beneficial to our rural population. Not only do they promote the local development of our raw materials, offer markets for some farm products, give employment to many workers and allow the use of local savings for the economic development of the area, but they help maintain a middle class which might become a great bulwark against subversive ideas. They keep in our small communities those who, in time of prosperity, would be dazzled by the great cities and those who, in time of depression, would increase the number of people looking for employment. Thus, by favouring the maintenance of an economic balance and the decentralization of industry and trade, they contribute to the accomplishment of a social work indispensable in a democratic country.
I humbly suggest to the government to give to that proposed board the most extended powers so that it may carry its investigations in our rural centres, find out what could be profitably produced there and bring conclusions whose implementation could promote the establishment of new businesses and the development of existing ones. Why not consider also the establishment of rural industrial credit which could supplement agricultural credit? As early as 1929 Belgium instituted a credit system of this type which contributed very efficiently to reducing the incidence of unemployment and maintaining the remarkable economic equilibrium which that country enjoys.


Mr. Speaker, the Quebec farmer is an element of resistance and of permanency on which the nation can count. A celebrated French economist, Andre Siegfried, once wrote:
By origin and by a tradition to which he remains faithful, he is a true countryman, devoted to the soil, retaining a sense of nature, whether it be a matter of cultivating the soil or of breaking new land.
It is in his person that we may find the old Canadian type preserved from outside contamination. He is rooted to the soil, through love of it as much as necessity. He wants to live on the land and from the land, to bring up his family there and perpetuate his name. He is an element of stability and order, he perpetuates tradition, a culture, a philosophy of life which constitutes an unsurmountable obstacle to Americanization in all its forms.
When in 1867 those who drafted our constitution agreed to form a confederation rather than a legislative union, they thought that in order to ensure the vigour and strength of the Canadian nation, it was necessary that the human type peculiar to our land should remain and perpetuate itself. He needed a legal framework in which he could realize all his potentialities. They thought further that the province he lived in should be endowed with institutions whereby he was to feel perfectly at home. That is why the 1867 constitution has such deep meaning for him that in the guarantees which it offers he finds the very condition of his existence, and that is why he is attached to it by all the fibres of his soul. This is for the Canadian nation a source of inexhaustible wealth. It is in this way that our country has peculiarities and general characteristics which have made of it something unique and incomparable. It has contributed to making it finer and greater.
In one of the brilliant talks which he gave at Oxford around 1926, Sir Robert Borden spoke out vigorously on this matter:
(Text):
-it was futile to expect in Canada the absorption of a virile people deeply attached to their language, their religion, and their traditions. Nor was it in the least desirable that such a fusion should take place. The qualities of the French and the English temperaments are in many respects complementary. Each is capable of distinctive service to the state and each has given it. Not in fusion but through co-operation the highest service of the two races can best be given to Canada.
(Translation):
Faithful to this principle, the present Prime Minister expressed the same thoughts in the

course of the last election campaign before an audience in the metropolis of Canada, when he said forcefully:
I know that one of the great forces of our country is that it can draw from the two greatest cultures of the modern world: the French culture and the English culture, to create a true Canadian spirit.
And he added those particularly significant words:
When I look at the great events of our history, I see no majority nor minorities in Canada but only equal partners engaged in the same undertaking, that of working for the welfare and progress of the country as a whole.
This philosophy, which is at the very source of the alliance which we Canadians of French culture and Canadians of English culture concluded in 1867, explains the attitude of the province of Quebec in the last elections.
After listening for too long to the voice of discord from a few of the very ones who then came here and professed to be champions of national unity, the province heard a voice which spoke words akin to its own ideas, its own feelings and its own aspirations. That voice preached precisely the kind of national unity which is dear to our hearts, the kind of national unity we must cultivate, the only one that can assure our country peace, stability and greatness.
It was the spirit of Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Georges-Etienne Cartier which blew again in the sails of the Conservative party, this spirit which fits in so well with the virtues of faithfulness, moderation and common sense characteristic of the people of Quebec and which, undoubtedly, will lead us to the realization of the ardent wish that, on the evening of election day, the Prime Minister expressed in French in the following words:
Together, French-speaking Canadians and Englishspeaking Canadians, we will write a new chapter of the history of Canada.
In the pursuit of this task to which the leader of the government called us, we Canadians of French culture believe, like the Prime Minister, that we have an essential part to play. Rooted in the soil for the past three and a half centuries, heirs to a culture which neither conquest, nor internal struggles, nor outside threats were able to uproot, descended by blood and spirit from one of the greatest civilizing nations of the world, we could not remain deaf to this call and stand aloof from the government of a country where we represent more than a third of the people.
We, Conservatives from the province of Quebec, have come here, therefore, in all
The Address-Mr. Roberge confidence and loyalty. In the very words of the right hon. Prime Minister, we want to be with our compatriots of English culture and language partners in the management of the country, in such a way that the rights and liberties of our two ethnic groups be respected and safeguarded, that our political institutions be pervaded with the spirit of the one and of the other and thus achieve at last this national unity for which all Canadians of good will have been yearning for so long.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with a mixed feeling of apprehension and satisfaction that a new member of parliament rises to take part in his first debate: apprehension because he does not know exactly what to expect and because he is not well acquainted with the atmosphere of the house; satisfaction because as you know, it is the achievement of a very legitimate ambition of whoever represents here his fellow-citizens.
I would ask you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, to convey to Mr. Speaker my most sincere congratulations on his election to the position he now occupies. I was not here last session, but I was able to follow the debates in the official report. I was able to appreciate the fairness and honesty of the decisions that Mr. Speaker made with such an adequate sense of humour. If such qualities were required during last session, I am convinced that they are even more needed in the present parliament to preserve the rights and privileges of the members of the opposition who sit to the immediate left of the Speaker.
I would be remiss if I did not mention, Mr. Deputy Speaker, your appointment to that post, as well as that of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Rea) to the post of deputy chairman of the committees. I knew you personally many years ago when we both were students of the revered seminary of Quebec where you earned your first laurels. We met again later when you were serving in the Canadian army and later again when you were seriously wounded. The eagerness with which you fought for liberty on the battlefield is a sure guarantee of the eagerness with which you will discharge your parliamentary duties.
The hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) must be commended for the speech he delivered in proposing the address in reply to the speech from the throne. You
346	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Roherge will, no doubt, appreciate, Mr. Speaker, that if a Liberal may admire the rhetoric of the proposer, this does not mean that he agrees with his reasoning and some of the political principles he stated.
I also wish to congratulate another young member, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen). I realize that like his leader, the Prime Minister, he had visions, but I am afraid that many a Canadian now settled farther south, and who is furthermore unemployed, will not be willing to follow the paths leading north.
Before making the few remarks I have in mind, may I, Mr. Speaker, put on the record a word of thanks and gratitude to the electors of my riding which I have the great honour of representing here. I want of course to thank particularly all those who, directly or indirectly, have assured my election to the House of Commons. I wish to add, however, that my ambition is to represent here not only the Liberals, but all the electors of the Megantic constituency without any distinction between parties or political creed. I will be constantly at their disposal, and I pledge them again my fullest devotion.
During the election campaign, Mr. Speaker, and since the beginning of this session, we have heard much about unemployment and about recession. Of course, statisticians and still less political speakers do not agree as to the number of unemployed in Canada. The fact is however that through last winter, their number was, and still is, much greater than at the same time in years past. It seems to me that their number is not decreasing as much as we would like.
Many steps have been advocated to bring about a sizeable reduction of the number of unemployed. Without ignoring the public works program announced by the right hon. Prime Minister, I believe that the idea of a tax reduction advocated by the hon. Leader of the Opposition, and particularly its implementation, would be much more likely to reach that goal. As a matter of fact, if we have a look at the list of those public works, we can see readily, as has been pointed out by many previous speakers, that they are regular and normal public works provided for in the yearly estimates. The Conservatives are certainly not the ones who started the tremendous works of the St. Lawrence seaway and much less the Trans-Canada pipe line, to name just those two. The carrying on of those projects and the start of others


cannot, I feel, help solve the problems completely, although the right hon. Prime Minister stated on several occasions, as was so pointedly mentioned by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill), that nobody would suffer from unemployment as long as he would head the Canadian government.
As we mentioned during the last election campaign, Canadians as a whole spend whatever is contained in their pay envelope. It is therefore imperative to increase the purchasing power of the Canadian taxpayers, and we believe that a huge cut in taxes would answer that purpose. If people buy more consumer goods, an increased production of such goods would necessarily follow, and as a consequence, there would be more jobs and a greater stability in employment.
The riding of Megantic, which I represent, Mr. Speaker, is partly urban and partly rural. As in all other parts of Canada, there is unemployment there, particularly, as you will understand, in the urban areas. I have not been able to get the accurate figures from the unemployment insurance officers, because part of the riding is served by the Victoriaville office, which is located in the riding of my hon. friend, the representative of Drummond-ville (Mr. Boulanger). Several parishes are under the jurisdiction of that office, so that it is not possible accurately to determine the extent of unemployment in my own riding. But I have before me the figures published on May 13, 1958 by the office in Thetford Mines, which serves a population of approximately 45,000. There are exactly 2,204 men and women looking for jobs, which is a very large number for this season. What public works does the government favour to check the recession and create employment for at least part of these twenty-two hundred jobless people? Thanks to the former government, amounts have been earmarked for the extension and improvement of the Thetford Mines post office. The work is now mostly finished and I must congratulate the government for implementing a project put foward by the former Liberal government.
I am aware also that the Liberal government of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent had appropriated some money for the building of a post office in Plessisville. The land was bought and tenders were called. According to some information which, I believe, is in the record of the debates of the last session, the contract had been granted

but later withdrawn, the latter event having occurred in the course of October. The session of last fall went by, the election was held and during that whole period nothing was done, as far as I know, toward the construction of that building during the winter unemployment period. It is only recently that new tenders were called. Judging by recent events, work will not start until next fall and yet this is the very time where unemployment is most serious, where construction workers find themselves without a job in that part of the constituency.
But what are the other public works which the government has in mind for the constituency of Megantic? I have heard nothing or seen nothing which can give me an inkling of its intentions in this regard.
You w'ill allow me, Mr. Speaker, to put forward a few suggestions for the appropriate department's consideration. In co-operation with the municipalities and in full and frank co-operation with the provincial government, the present federal government should establish a municipal lending fund which would help municipalities carry out important and useful public works.
I know many municipalities in my riding which would welcome that government assistance. I suppose that, now that political relations are closer between the federal government and the provincial government, co-operation will be easier than it has been.
To give a concrete example, the government could study the possibility of providing the constituency of Megantic either with an airport or with an helicopter station. As a matter of fact, Megantic stands about midway between Quebec and Sherbrooke, about 150 miles from Montreal. Major public works would help, at least partially, to alleviate unemployment and would contribute to the development of means of transportation in that area.
We have already dealt during this session with unemployment insurance. I do not wish to criticize the stand taken by the government in connection with some supplementary benefits, but I find in the speech delivered by His Excellency on May 12 last that the government intends to bring other amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act. I would like to offer a few suggestions one of which in particular has been submitted to me by some electors of my riding.
As a general rule, ordinary or seasonal benefits are now paid to workers who are
The Address-Mr. Roberge on the labour market looking for work. Such benefits have been extended by the former Liberal government to those who, while they were without work, fell ill. It seems to me that we should consider extending benefits to those who lose their job on account of illness; then their families would not have them to worry about the difficulties they have to go through in such circumstances.
I also believe that unemployment insurance benefits should be extended to another group of people. According to the existing legislation of most of the provinces, the widow and children cf a workman killed on the job are entitled to a pension but when this workman dies from illness or from any other kind of accident, to my knowledge no legislation provides for a pension to his surviving dependants. In many cases, the workman has paid unemployment insurance contributions for several years and never had to draw any kind of benefits. A system of unemployment insurance could be instituted whereby the widow of a deceased workman could draw benefits on behalf of her deceased husband for a certain time, at least until she has adjusted herself to her new conditions. In my opinion, the government should take this problem under serious consideration, as it could affect a certain proportion of the people, and provide a solution in the sense I have just indicated.
Without criticizing the legislation concerning the extension of unemployment insurance seasonal benefits, I must point out that those who stopped receiving benefits before May 17, 1958, do not draw any more money under the new legislation. I suggest that the government remedy the situation when the other changes announced in the speech from the throne of His Excellency are submitted to the house.
(Text):
Having now dealt with the unemployment situation in Canada, Mr. Speaker, and the situation in that respect in my own constituency, I would like to say a few words about those who are not yet ready for employment. I refer to the children of our country.
If I now address you, sir, in the other official language used in this country, it is probably due to the fact that the simultaneous translation system has not yet been introduced in this house-as far as I can see, anyway. During the recent election campaign I heard over television the Solicitor

The Address-Mr. Roberge General declare that his government had caused an act to be passed in this regard. I would very much like to know the reference to that act, if the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Balcer) would care to give it.
Coming back to the children of this country, I would like to point out that the government has done nothing since it took office with regard to the question of family allowances. If the cost of living has risen for the elderly people, the crippled and the blind, I cannot see how it did not also rise for the children of the country, and more particularly for those responsible for them.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the government should improve family allowances in favour of our children, not only those who are very young, but those who are old enough to attend school. Since the adoption of this family allowances system by former Liberal governments, many improvements and additions have been made to it, without in any way upsetting the budget. It is to be noted, however, that this field of social legislation seems to be the only one about which the government did not think at all. I believe it is imperative that the government should think about it. In what proportion should these family allowances be increased? That is up to the government to decide.
I should like to draw particular attention, however, to one category of young people in this country who do not benefit at present from family allowances. I am referring to those children of both sexes who continue to attend school after age sixteen, and who do so until they are eighteen. These young people were, as was advocated by the Liberal party, to receive family allowances in the same way as those who now receive them, and at least on the same scale.
Several of these young people, when they reach eighteen or pass their B.A. want to continue their studies at the university level. I know I am broaching a delicate issue, particularly with regard to the province of Quebec which keeps a jealous watch of its prerogatives in the matter of education. The problem may now seem easier to solve and the co-operation between the central government and the Quebec government might be more efficient in view of the active proof of friendship we recently witnessed.
The right to education belongs first of all to our children and should not depend on the


financial means of their parents but on the young people's talent and future opportunities. With regard to this right there is, of course a corresponding obligation on behalf of parents to provide this education. The state however should play a supplementary part, which belongs in the first place to the provinces.
However, in 1958, when science is fast developing, when artificial moons circle around the earth, when long range missiles can be launched farther and farther, education is becoming more and more an intercontinental problem, and at least an interprovincial problem. I do not see any reason why the central power should not contribute its share in this field, without infringing upon the rights of parents and of the provinces.
If we must give assistance to the children who want to go to university, it is also imperative to assist our universities themselves, which at the present time all complain of lack of funds.
In this respect, the Liberal government of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent had provided a sizeable financial help to universities; but, unfortunately, the universities of my province have been able to benefit from those grants only once.
The Prime Minister said in Saskatchewan, not so long ago, that his government would assist the universities of that province. I figure that his statement was not a restricted one, and that, as a consequence, all Canadian provinces can take for granted that their universities will receive their share. I hope that the Quebec universities will be able at last to receive what they are entitled to, and I urge the Prime Minister, as well as his colleagues from the province of Quebec, to see that the governmental authorities of my province co-operate at last towards the solution of this national problem, in the future, and thereby contribute to the welfare of our universities.
As far as the children are concerned, the federal government could, while respecting the autonomy of the provinces as well as the rights of the parents in the field of education, as I have already said, give substantial assistance to those who have talent, as well as the will to succeed and to prepare adequately for the future. This government help could well be implemented through the agency of the national conference of Canadian universities. The government would then have no control whatever over anything save over the amounts which it could put at the disposal of that conference.

Here, Mr. Speaker, are the Liberal party suggestions with regard to these student scholarships and loans.
1.	Establish a large scale national scholarship program for university students. These scholarships would be granted through a public competition held in the two official languages of this country, under the control of the national conference of Canadian universities.
2.	To supplement this scholarship program, a national fund would be set up so as to allow students to obtain loans in order to pursue their university studies.
This government should study the advisability of carrying out this program, thus solving at least in part a very important problem.
Before concluding, I wish to express the sense of deep satisfaction I felt seeing my leader carry an electoral campaign with such vigour under very trying circumstances and not more than fifteen days after his election as our party leader.
I noted with great pleasure that during this campaign he showed special concern for our university students, meeting them in their universities to discuss their problems with them. I offer him my special congratulations for this solicitude toward those who are preparing Canada's future while preparing their own.

Mr. Speaker, I consider it a real privilege to add my congratulations to yourself and to your deputy, and also to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I should like heartily to endorse the remarks made by the hon. member for Yukon, having spent some considerable number of years in the Yukon myself.
The constituency of Wetaskiwin, which was established in 1905, for 37 years sent representatives to Ottawa who sat on the wrong side of the house. This is the first time in its 53-year history that this constituency has sent a Progressive Conservative member to parliament. The constituency which I have the honour to represent is essentially agricultural, although in the past 10 years we have risen to the position of producing over 25 per cent of Alberta's oil. Our principal agricultural products are, however, diversified, so much so that the disposal of surplus grain presents no problem in this constituency.
To turn to oil, the present import restriction imposed by our neighbour to the south has, of course, created some unemployment.
The Address-Mr. Speakman Those engaged in our oil industry are for the most part young men proud of their ability to work. However, these young men feel a high degree of confidence that this government will do all that lies in its power to bring about an easing of these restrictions and thus provide for continuous employment.
At the present time the markets for our agricultural products are very good and prices are very high. Increased livestock production in my constituency has led to the ending of the problem of surplus grain, because we feed not only our grain but to a considerable extent grain produced in adjoining constituencies. Dairying is one of our major activities in these constituencies. Our Wetaskiwin branch of the northern Alberta dairy pool is a consistent winner of prizes for butter production. Our surplus dairy products go, in the main, to the central Alberta dairy pool plant at Red Deer, a condensory which is continually increasing its output. Production from this condensory fluctuates seasonally, and during the period of heavy production a surplus is built up at the plant. We feel that some support should be given to this product in order to keep production at a high level and enable the plant to compete in the export market with the larger producers.
I would like to read figures to show the importance of this industry to central Alberta. The quantity of evaporated milk we have for export would be equal to approximately 500,000 pounds of skim milk powder and 250,000 pounds of butter. This government has put price supports on both skim milk powder and butter. I would suggest to the government and principally to the Minister of Agriculture that he give consideration to placing a support on the price of evaporated milk, which would permit this plant to compete with the larger producers in the export market.
As in other agricultural constituencies our agricultural population is decreasing, and we welcome this government's suggested amendments to the Canadian Farm Loan Act. A large portion of my constituency is in the marginal and submarginal soil areas where an expansion of farm credit will do much to assist in the modernization and developing of the farms and thus keep our young men on the farms so they will not swell the ranks of the unemployed in the urban centres. We have in Canada today a well-trained staff immediately available to implement any amendments brought in to the Canadian Farm Loan Act, in the field staffs under the Veterans' Land Act. In my opinion no country has such a highly trained staff in agriculture so immediately available.
It is in my constituency that the Hobbema and Ma Me O Indian reserves lie. Doubtless

The Address-Mr. Badanai the word "Hobbema" will have a familiar ring to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, the former minister of citizenship and immigration. The acceleration of educational and other facilities to hasten the eventual integration of these people into full citizenship in Canada will be welcomed in this constituency and amongst these bands.
I must at this point mention the admiration I feel for the churches in the work they have done in educational and other matters amongst the Indian bands.
It is a matter of great pride to me to have come to this house as an elected representative of some of the people of Alberta. My constituency of Wetaskiwin adjoins the constituency of Red Deer from which my uncle was elected to this house in 1921. It is my sincere hope that I can give to the people of my constituency, the people of Alberta and the people of Canada the representation that was given by my late uncle, Alfred Speakman, to his people whom he served for 15 years between 1921 and 1935.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my first contribution to the debates of this house I should like to exercise the degree of modesty becoming a new member, a modesty which will not overlook, however, certain facts concerning the constituency which I have the honour to represent. My words are not words of wisdom; they are simply the voice of a student rather than that of an expert. It may not be necessary, therefore, for me to take up the whole 40 minutes allotted to speakers on the speech from the throne. As a matter of fact, if I may express an humble opinion, these speeches could be limited to 20 minutes save and except by leave of the house or when circumstances warrant a longer period, such as when the Prime Minister speaks, or the Leader of the Opposition.
At the outset I wish to extend my personal congratulations to you, sir, for being selected for the most important position in the house, because we believe you represent the very embodiment of fair play so necessary in the conduct of this honourable parliament. I also wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Lafre-niere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne for their excellent presentations, and especially do I wish to congratulate the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for the masterly way in which he presented the viewpoint of Her Majesty's loyal opposition urging the government to adopt a policy designed to increase the level of international trade by introducing vigorous measures for the expansion of the exchange of goods and services with as many countries of the world as possible.

This is a sure way of helping, if not curing entirely, our present unemployment situation, which notwithstanding all the oratory we have heard to the contrary continues to loom as a serious problem. I have just received a telegram from the director of the national employment office at Fort William confirming the fact that there are still 2,445 unemployed people in that city. Had it not been for the work of the winter employment committee which conducted a successful "do it now" campaign throughout the winter months the figures of unemployed persons would be much higher. I wish to pay tribute to all of those who served on this committee.
Lest I should unwittingly convey a pessimistic outlook concerning the future of Canada I hasten to assure the house that there is no depression in my vision, but I do wish to say there is much room for improvement, and the government has the power and the opportunity to bring about measures which will be beneficial to Canadians everywhere. I believe this can be accomplished if the government will act on suggestions coming from this side of the house, for let it not be said that all the brains of the country are confined to the right side of Mr. Speaker.
During the past few days we have had the pleasure of listening to several fine addresses. They were, by and large, notable commentaries which reflected the thinking of many widely separated areas of Canada, and I in turn am very appreciative of the opportunity of bringing to the attention of the house some of the problems besetting my riding as well as our hopes for better days. In his speech on the address a few days ago the hon. member for York West (Mr. Hamilton) made the following statement, as found at page 49 of Hansard of May 13:
May I say that I hope the day of the personality cult in connection with the administration of our foreign affairs is over . . .
If there has ever been a personality cult in evidence in Canada, Mr. Speaker, I respectfully submit that the present Prime Minister would certainly be head and shoulders above any other candidate because of the admiration showered upon him by his supporters as though he were a Caesar. In fairness to the Prime Minister, I believe it is quite possible that he is a victim of his own popularity, which was exploited rather successfully by his party during the last election campaign.
(Translation):
As it appears to be in order for Englishspeaking members to say a few words in French, one of our two official languages, I undertook this agreeable task with the help of some friends.

I am very much impressed by the friendly attitude of all hon. members, to whatever party they belong.
I am beginning to realize that, if the teaching of French was mandatory at the various levels of our schools, it would be a wonderful thing for Canada. I venture to hope that this will come about in the not too distant future. (Text):
The speech from the throne foreshadowed a busy agenda for this session of parliament. It contained some excellent suggestions, with many of which I am in full accord, especially the one dealing with the establishment of a harbour commission for the lakehead cities of Port Arthur and Fort William and the preparing of that harbour to handle ocean going ships. I had hoped that the speech would at least contain a reference to the plight of the municipalities with regard to the difficulties they face in obtaining loans for municipal improvements at low rates of interest, especially in view of the submission made to the government on February 7 last by the executive of the Canadian federation of mayors and municipalities.
The borrowing capacity of municipalities is necessarily limited, and it is therefore imperative that if they are to continue to provide essential local services the federal government should establish a national loan fund-thus being of inestimable assistance- from which the municipalities would borrow at the federal bond rate of interest to finance projects approved by provincial municipal boards. These boards are the watchdogs of municipal expenditures, serving as a protective force against unwise spending on nonessential projects.
With respect to housing, the speech contained the promise of a vigorous program of house building. However, the legislation adopted in the house last week did not go far enough. My own view is that the government should subsidize interest rates on mortgage loans for houses costing less than $12,000. Anybody who is able to afford a new house costing over $12,000 should be able to meet the going market interest rate. Houses, including site costs, under $12,000 are today in the low cost category and a subsidy of say 2 per cent would bring the effective rate of interest to about 4 per cent.
One of the crying needs of the moment is houses for rent. In our municipality we have taken advantage of the former government's housing scheme introduced in 1950 or 1951, and I was pleased to see that the present government is carrying on with the same formula of 75 per cent federal investment and 25 per cent split between the province and
The Address-Mr. Badanai the municipality. The only trouble is that the scheme, while good, should provide for an increase in the federal government's share of the cost of acquiring and clearing substandard areas for low rental housing projects.
I sincerely hope that the Prime Minister will convene a federal-provincial-municipal conference some time during 1958. Such a conference could accomplish much to solve the problems involved in the growth and development of our urban communities. The municipalities cannot be ignored by the federal government. The complexities of our modern age demand a reassessment of the field of responsibilities of all levels of government.
The speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, did not make any reference to government policy on immigration, and this is a rather important omission. In view of Canada's economic prospects for the future, as forecast by the royal commission, and even accepting the fact that Canadian women are doing their duty by maintaining the birth rate at a high level, there is substantial evidence to indicate the desirability of selective and steady immigration if Canada is to achieve its destiny as a truly great nation, to say nothing of the great vision of the development of the north so dramatically portrayed by the Prime Minister during the election campaign.
In this connection I wish to submit for the consideration of the government a proposal to establish a policy of bringing in emigrants from any land who will qualify as farmers and who will settle on the land, especially in undeveloped areas such as northwestern Ontario. Specifically I mean in the area adjacent to the city of Fort William, where we have a vast potential of good land for mixed farming. These prospective settlers would be required to sign an agreement to remain on the land for at least five years, and if they should fail to live up to the contract they would be subject to deportation. This policy would prevent crowding of the labour market and would thus create more jobs for industrial workers, who would be kept busy producing and manufacturing for these new consumers. In order to make such a scheme succeed the government should establish a loan fund from which these immigrants would be able to borrow for long terms and at a low rate of interest. This loan fund should also operate for the benefit of established farmers who wish to improve their holdings.
The speech from the throne indicated a desire to assist small business. With this I am in full agreement, and I would add that this classification should include tourist operators, who should be allowed to participate in any loan fund legislation the government

The Address-Mr. Badanai introduces to assist small business. At the present time it is almost impossible tor a tourist operator to keep his establishment up to the standard desired by the department of travel and publicity because he is unable to obtain a loan from banks, mortgage companies or government sources.
The tourist business is considered the third largest business in Canada, pouring hundreds of millions of dollars into the country annually, yet there is practically no form of assistance to it. One large operator in my city recently stated to me that under certain conditions a farmer could get a loan to instal a water system for his pigs, but as motel operator it was not possible for him to borrow sufficient funds to put respectable washroom facilities in his establishment for human beings.
Some of you may ask why I am so interested in the tourist business. The reason is that Fort William and the lakehead area is a real vacationland paradise. The splendor of the scenery is such that I have heard Scottish people say it was a constant reminder to them of Fort William, Scotland, and of the gorgeous bonnie Prince Charles country. This region was practically free of polio even before the advent of the Salk vaccine, and it is a wonderland for hay fever sufferers. There are hundreds of inland lakes, many yet unfished by white men because of a lack of access roads. This lack of roads presents the government with an opportunity to implement promises made during the election campaign.
From time to time, Mr. Speaker, Fort William received assurance that consideration would be given to the construction of a new armoury. The site was made available by the city and arrangements made for the use of the land occupied by the old building. The present armoury building has been condemned as a fire hazard by the fire chief, whose action was supported by the fire marshal of Ontario. Is it the intention of the Department of National Defence to construct a new armoury in Fort William, or must this old building, which was once an arena, continue to be a menace to the business section of the city?
We are somewhat disturbed over the amount of protection the lakehead area can expect in the event of a nuclear war. We cannot agree with the designated role of our cities as a "stand fast" area. We have co-operated in every way possible with civil defence authorities, but always with the reservation that Fort William and Port Arthur are not being called upon to protect the vast food supplies that are stored there. Sufficient thought is not being given to the

proper protection of a vital area. We are in agreement with most cities that civil defence preparedness is not realistic, that the federal government is encouraging apathy amongst the general public and, more important, is actually discouraging a large nucleus of important key personnel from doing a job. A tidal wave of paper is being turned out by the queen's printer which is filled with vague promises and contradictory and misleading suppositions.
Civil defence is the most important service we can provide for the protection of our people, if proper leadership and guidance are given. We are not alone in the civil defence field. Other countries have made far greater progress, why can't we? Surely it is not too costly to provide a proper warning system for every city in Canada. Pumper trucks should be provided by the government for every isolated area, and indeed for all mutual aid areas. Many municipalities cannot afford to provide this equipment, yet it is essential that protection be given. The government should regard civil defence as first-line defence, and be prepared for anything in this nuclear age.
The development of a deep sea harbour at the lakehead is vital to the growth and prosperity of the whole of Canada. For years Fort William and Port Arthur fulfilled their role as the breadbasket of the world. Millions of bushels of grain and millions of tons of iron ore from Steep Rock iron mines have been shipped through the lakehead harbours annually. As far back as 1655 Fort William played an important role in the economy of the nation. At that time the French explorers Radisson and Des Groseil-liers visited the area. In 1678 Daniel Greysolon Dulhut established a fur trading post, and now this whole region stands on the threshold of huge expansion.
It was no surprise to me to hear in the speech from the throne the recommendation that a harbour commission for the lakehead be established. The lakehead is important to the economy of the North American continent because it is a natural gateway to the west and in the centre of the whole continent. Its destiny has been portrayed as the Chicago of the north, and I am sure that destiny will be achieved. The amount of shipping through lakehead ports exceeded that of Toronto and Hamilton by over one million tons in 1957. I was glad to see, as my hon. friends must have seen, an editorial in the Globe and Mail of May 20 referring to the lakehead. It is headed "New Look for the Lakehead", and reads:
A weak spot in Canada's St. Lawrence seaway planning until recently has been the lakehead ports -Fort William and Port Arthur. It has been obvious from the beginning that if the project was

to fulfil its great economic promise to the nation as a whole, and to western Canada in particular, the lakehead ports would have to undergo great improvements-organizational and physical.
The lakehead harbours are 1,250 miles from Montreal by water or 2,250 miles from the open Atlantic ocean. The impact of the seaway will be stimulating to trade and industrial expansion, and will increase the lake-head importance as a distribution centre. However, in order to accelerate this development it is essential that the extension of the breakwater be undertaken by the Department of Public Works as soon as possible. Ocean ships are not unique at the lakehead. They have been calling at these ports for many years, but the deepening of the channels and the seaway will permit much larger ships to penetrate the heart of the Canadian hinterland. It will mean cheaper rates for export grain and will eliminate cargo transfer between the lakehead and Montreal. The estimates are that this may mean as much as 5 cents a bushel.
Natural gas, which is now available at the lakehead, will provide employment for thousands. Notwithstanding all that was said in the famous pipe-line debate of 1956, had it not been for the courage and determination of the former Liberal government to put the bill through this gas would still be under the ground or going to waste instead of enriching our economy. The availability of gas will make it possible for an iron ore processing plant to be established in the lakehead area. The processing of iron ore by gas is a revolutionary new method. Such an iron ore processing plant would make Canada independent of other countries, particularly the United States, and I understand that iron and steel products are largely responsible for our large trade deficit with that country.
I would suggest that the support of the federal government to establish an iron ore processing plant at Fort William would be beneficial to the whole country.
As a prophet, Mr. Speaker, I am not in the same class as some of my hon. friends on the other side of the house. However,
I venture to predict that within the next 25 years the lakehead area will witness dynamic development into one of Canada's greatest, a mighty pillar supporting the economic progress of our nation. The Prime Minister has not misplaced his confidence in recognizing the need of preparing the lake-head for the coming of the seaway.
With the exception of the newest members of the house, every one here knew my good friend and distinguished predecessor, Rev. Dan Mclvor, who for 23 years represented the riding of Fort William in this house.
The Address-Mr. Stewart I am sure this chamber has seen many members endowed with ability and honesty of purpose, but I doubt whether anyone has ever occupied one of these chairs who could even approach the humanity of the former hon. member for Fort William. I know you would want me to convey to him on your behalf greetings and best wishes for a long, healthy and enjoyable retirement with Mrs. Mclvor, a gracious and beloved lady well known in Ottawa. Finally, I wish to express my deepest gratitude to my constituents for the privilege and opportunity to serve them here.
I wish to conclude with a legend concerning an old Indian chief. This chief was growing very old and, feeling that the end was near, he wished to select someone among his braves to succeed him. So he called all the braves of his tribe together and from among them he selected four whom he thought worthy to carry on the traditions of his forebears. To them he said, "Tomorrow morning at sunrise you will climb yonder mountain: you will climb as high as you can, but you must return at sunset". The following morning the four braves started out and at sunset they returned. Of the first one the old chief asked, "How high did you climb?", and the brave answered, "I saw the spruce". Of the second the old chief asked, "How high did you climb?", and the brave replied, "I saw the pine". To the third the old chief put the same question and the answer came, "I saw the alpine brush". Finally of the fourth the old chief asked, "How high did you climb?" Proudly the brave answered, "I saw the sea".
After confederation 91 years ago, under the great Sir John A. Macdonald Canada climbed to the spruce. She climbed to the pine under the great Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Under Borden and Meighen she climbed to the alpine brush; and under the inspired leadership of Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent she climbed until she saw the sea.
God grant that during the next four or five years under the Prime Minister, John Diefenbaker, Canada may continue on the road to development, prosperity and security for all Canadians.

I would like at this time, Mr. Speaker, to extend a word of appreciation to the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Although separated by a great distance geographically these two gentlemen have two things in common, youth and a manifest desire to assist the people who have sent them to this parliament.
As one of the members from New Brunswick I would like on behalf of the people of that province and the people of my own constituency in particular to voice our appreciation of the magnificent work done by the Minister of Veterans Affairs. He has at all times lent a very sympathetic and considerate ear to our problems. I would also like, on behalf of the people of my constituency, to voice a word of appreciation of the work of the Department of Public Works in my area during the past few months, for the work that is contemplated and for the work that will be done in the next year or so.
I was rather surprised to find that some of the members of the opposition were opposed to the program of public works outlined. It is very significant that the great republic to the south is now engaged on such projects to assist in the current unemployment situation. I can speak with some authority, as during
the period 1944-45 I was engaged as an engineer by the Department of Public Works, operating out of the Saint John office. At that time we were engaged in what was known as the post-war planning development. Unfortunately that scheme was dropped, so that when this depression or recession came about we had no shelf of public works available to us. I know that it is not possible to start public works projects overnight. Surveys must be carried out, plans must be made and estimates obtained, all as preliminary steps to the actual work being started, and had the Liberal government prior to June 10, 1957, established such a shelf of works, then I am sure we would not have had the difficulties we experienced during last summer.
I do not wish the Minister of Public Works or the Minister of Transport to become too complacent about this matter, because I am sure they will find there are still many projects awaiting their attention in my constituency, and if I should be insistent and impatient I hope they will realize 1 am only trying to better conditions for the people I represent.
I would also like on behalf of the people of Charlotte to renew our pledges of loyalty and devotion to the Prime Minister. My words are most inadequate to express to him our feelings for what he has done for our constituency and for the people of New Brunswick generally. While my predecessor was in this house and during the period between the second world war and the 1957 election nothing was done to assist the maritime provinces or the province of New Brunswick in particular. When we asked for power or the money to develop power we were told that we did not have any industries requiring power. When we asked for industries we were told the reverse, that we had no power with which to provide industry.
The present Prime Minister, however, realized the inequalities under which the maritimes area was operating and very generously persuaded his government to make additional grants over and above the amounts called for under the tax rental agreements, and I am sure that was greatly appreciated by the people of my constituency. He has, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion blazed a path of hope across the face of the maritimes which neither time nor political fortunes will ever erase. He has given to the people of the Atlantic area a new hope, a new courage for the future, and I am sure those people, along with the people of the rest of Canada, will join with him in bringing to fulfilment his national policy for our country.
I represent a small constituency in terms of population. It is bounded on the south by

three islands and the bay of Fundy, on the west by the state of Maine, on the north by York-Sunbury and on the east by Saint John-Albert. Although the great majority of my people are fishermen or are engaged in the fishing industry, and for that reason require special consideration, I want to tell this house that they are among the finest people in the world; and I can say that without blowing my own trumpet as I am not a native of Charlotte. It has been my privilege during the past 18 years, however, first as an engineer during the war and then as a practising lawyer, to live among them; and I can assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I speak from the bottom of my heart when I say I am proud to represent these people in this house, and that I know they are deserving of better consideration than they have received in the past.

During the period since the second world war several economic changes have taken place in my constituency which have been very detrimental to the peace and security of the people there. I do not entirely blame these changes on political considerations, but it is significant that since 1945, when my predecessor came to this house, great calamity has descended on my constituents. First there was the closing of the Pennfield airport, which in my opinion was closed entirely for political reasons. Then prior to the 1957 election there was the closing of the textile mill at Milltown.
I want to bring to the attention of this house the plight of the people of Milltown. They will shortly run out of all unemployment insurance benefits, and we will have approximately 600 families out of work in that town.
I was rather interested to learn that within the last few days the province of Nova Scotia has decided to build a textile mill in the depressed area of Pictou county, costing approximately $100,000, which they will rent to a textile firm from Italy for the purpose of carrying on manufacturing. Surely this government, in co-operation with the government of New Brunswick, can do something for the town of Milltown, and I am bringing this matter to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and also to the attention of Mr. Pichette, minister of industry and development in the province of New Brunswick.
We had a third change, also. That was the closing of the army camp at Utopia. During the last campaign that camp was a major issue in the election, but my worthy opponent and my predecessor knew that
57071-3-23J
The Address-Mr. Stewart when the decision was made by his government to make a permanent camp of Camp Gagetown, camp Utopia as an army base would be closed. I have hopes that the facilities and buildings of that camp can still be used for the betterment of the people of my constituency, and plans are now being discussed with the province of New Brunswick whereby this camp may be utilized, thereby avoiding it being a total loss.
I have referred to these three things as affecting the economy of Charlotte county. In 1931 the number of people in New Brunswick living on farms amounted to 44.1 per cent of the total population, but in 1956 this dropped to 23.3 per cent. In 1931 the farm population in New Brunswick was 180,000, while in 1956 in round figures it was 128,000. A corresponding decrease was noted in my constituency where the farm population now stands, according to the latest available figures, at 1,872, occupying 469 farms.
According to the latest available figures from the department of industry and development of the province of New Brunswick, the gross value of manufactured production for 1954 was $287,350,000; and in the breakdown of that table, Mr. Speaker, we notice that the fish processing industry consists of 166 plants employing 2,742 people with a gross value in 1955 of approximately $23 million for the whole province of New Brunswick.
Many hon. members of this house will remember the opposition voiced by my predecessor when the province of New Brunswick obtained the loan toward the Beechwood power development. Whether or not the Beechwood project is sound from an engineering viewpoint, it was certainly not part of my predecessor's duty to oppose it, because it was certainly for the benefit of New Brunswick.
There is another field in which I am vitally interested, and that is the field of education. At the present time I hold the position of president of the New Brunswick school trustees' association. During the last 10 years the cost of education has increased in Charlotte county by 128 per cent, throwing an enormous burden on the municipality. This is a very important consideration for this government, and I am hoping that in some way the Dominion of Canada may see its way clear to advancing additional grants to the province of New Brunswick and to the various municipalities so the burden may be removed from, the tax-ridden local authorities.
The speech from the throne indicated some of the proposed legislation, but it is not allinclusive, and other proposals beneficial to the dominion could be introduced I was-

The Address-Mr. Stewart very interested, as a practising lawyer, in the contemplated bill of rights. As I mentioned before, I have been practising law for 25 years, and in some instances I have found that individual freedom and liberty has been curtailed under our new system of jurisprudence. I think there should be a return to those fundamental rights which were granted to our forefathers and enjoyed by our predecessors; that no one should be dispossessed of his land or punished without a fair trial by his peers. These are matters which cannot be expressed in terms of dollars; they go to the very root of democracy and are the very lifeblood of civilization.
I am pleased to note that an amendment has been adopted extending the period of seasonal benefits under the Unemployment Insurance Act. May I suggest to the Minister of Fisheries that a further amendment be made to provide greater benefits to the fishermen of the maritime area, particularly to those men who are fishermen as well as owners.
The making available of funds under the National Housing Act is also a step in the right direction, because without homes people cannot live. May I suggest for the consideration of this house that we should also establish small industries in various municipalities and communities so that people will be encouraged to enter those communities and live there, setting up homes and raising families.
These are some of the problems facing the people of my constituency. These people do not wish me to come before this house begging; we are not asking for anything we do not deserve. We are asking that we be included once again within New Brunswick and within Canada. My worthy opponent, my predecessor in this house, told Upper Canada, when speaking here on one occasion, that the people of Charlotte were nothing but a bunch of smugglers. That is hardly true. We live, it is true, near the United States border and to some extent certain American influence bears upon the islands. But, as I said before, these are the finest people in the world and they are only asking that they be treated as human beings.
We have great potentialities in Charlotte. We have many tourist attractions, and all we need is a little assistance and help. We now have a great power development in the process of investigation, the Quoddy project, by means of which the tides of the bay of Fundy will be harnessed to make cheap power. We have also, on Campobello island, the old home of the late Franklin D. Roosevelt, which could be made into an important tourist attraction.

I mentioned earlier that we had three islands. One of these islands will shortly be joined to the state of Maine by a bridge which will give to the people of Campobello some of the benefits enjoyed on the mainland. However, the island of Grand Manan is desperately in need of a new ferry with adequate facilities for the transportation of automobiles and cargo.
These are matters which will be mentioned in this house and brought to the attention of the government. All we ask is that we should receive co-operation and assistance so that together with the other maritime areas we can go along with the Prime Minister in his policy of developing the national economy.

Mr. Speaker, may I join with other hon. members on both sides of the house in extending to you my sincere congratulations upon your re-election to your high office. I was delighted to hear the Prime Minister mention your name when it came to the appointment of a Speaker. I am sure that all hon. members who were in this house last session were impressed by the manner in which you presided over our deliberations. There may have been other Speakers who were, perhaps, more technically-minded than yourself, but I am sure there was no Speaker who was more fair-minded or more human and understanding than Your Honour, and it is with pleasure that I offer you my congratulations and best wishes.
( Translation):
Mr. Speaker, I also want to congratulate the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere) on having moved in such eloquent terms the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I also imagine that the hon. member does not expect me entirely to share his political views but, even while not sharing them, I may at least say that I respect them.
