(Text):
I should also like to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) on the way he seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I listened with interest to the very interesting speech he made on the northland, and I hope the house will have an opportunity to listen to him often this session.
Now that the election campaign is over and the dust has settled somewhat I indeed want to congratulate the Prime Minister and the members of the government on having won the confidence of the Canadian people and on having obtained not only a mandate but a great majority in the House of Commons. Such a vote of confidence is certainly an

enviable tribute, of which any Prime Minister and any political party might well be proud. But of course, underlying this tribute of the Canadian people there is the feeling of great expectation of things to come, and I sincerely hope the government will be successful in implementing all its policies and promises and that the policies themselves will prove to be effective and in the best interests of the Canadian people.
As a result of the last election the House of Commons has lost from the three opposition parties a great number of sincere and competent, and in some cases brilliant, parliamentarians who have made indelible marks in the political, economic and social structure of our country, and to whom Canada owes a great debt of gratitude. It might be timely to remind the Canadian people that there is nothing shameful, nothing disgraceful and nothing personal for a man in public life to experience defeat in an election campaign and it would indeed be wrong not to pay tribute to those hon. members who have gone down to defeat after many years, in some cases after a lifetime, in the service of their country in the very exacting, largely misunderstood and frequently thankless position of member of parliament.
Canada apparently is now witnessing the end of a political era and the beginning of another, and I feel quite sure every hon. member on either side of the house in looking back over the last quarter century of our country's history will feel justifiable pride in the rapid and extensive steps Canada has taken in its march toward nationhood. I feel quite certain that no country in the world can boast of having developed so much in such a short time. The jobless and poverty stricken people of Canada of the depression era now enjoy the second highest standard of living in the world. From a practically exclusively agricultural country we have developed an efficient and powerful industrial machine and have become the world's fourth largest trading nation. No country in the world of 17 million population enjoys as extensive and comprehensive social legislation as does Canada. In spite of world war II, the economic difficulties of the post-war years and the Korean war the Canadian economy did not falter. Prosperity and employment continued at reasonably stable levels, and there was no serious and lasting post-war recession.
In the international field where world trade, international diplomacy and world peace affect our country more than at any other period of our history, Canada evolved from an internationally isolated and unknown country to take the lead among the middlesized nations of the world. As a matter of
The Address-Mr. Cardin fact Canada as a middle-sized nation has not only effectively supported peace organizations such as NATO and the United Nations, but Canada actually was instrumental in avoiding a third world war during the Suez crisis. I am indeed proud to remind the house that it was the present Leader of the Opposition in his capacity as secretary of state for external affairs who through his tireless, courageous and timely negotiations succeeded in maintaining peace by establishing the United Nations emergency force in the Middle East. With all due respect to the Minister of Transport may I say that the present Leader of the Opposition accomplished this without the estimable help of the present very capable and versatile Prime Minister.
As Canada enters a new political era under a Conservative government the House of Commons presents a practically new slate of members with an average age group apparently lower than it has been for many years. I feel confident, however, that the new members will be able to pick up and carry on where the older and more experienced members of the house left off. There are, of course, new standards to be achieved, new adjustments to be made and new solutions to old problems to be tried out, as more particularly set forth in the government's policy platform and promises. One of these main problems to my mind will be an economic readjustment. I am afraid that Canada will face much stiffer competition in the world and the home markets. Somehow there will have to be a halt to the continually rising prices in our country if we expect to sell our products at home and abroad and maintain the stable economy we have known until now. There will also have to be some serious readjustment of Canada's trading position in view of the probable creation of economic blocs such as the European customs union which I believe will characterize the new era as the political and military bloc characterized the last decade or so. I strongly suspect that the battles between east and west will be fought in the economic and scientific fields rather than in the military field. All this, of course, will not make it any easier for anyone charged with the administration of the country's business.
It might be useful to remind ourselves that it is the earnest desire, the ardent hope and indeed the duty of each member of the house to do his best to ensure that the legislation passed during this present parliament will meet successfully the various problems of these times and will result in even greater economic, political and social stability and progress than we have known in the past. It is quite clear from the speeches and policy declarations made during the campaign that

The Address-Mr. Cardin we will not always agree on the best way of achieving a universally desired objective, and of course under our parliamentary system members of the opposition have not only a right but an obligation to be constructively critical of the government's actions in such a way that the public may be informed of as many solutions to the problems as possible.
During this parliament the government with 208 members has an overwhelming majority over the 57 total official opposition members, but this in no way should imply a diminution or decrease in the rights and privileges to which the opposition is entitled by the constitution, the traditions and the rules and practices of this house. The rights and privileges that were claimed by hon. members opposite when they were the official opposition are equally justified today, and I believe they should be guarded more jealously and more scrupulously than at any other time in our history precisely because of the government's record majority.
It is certainly to be hoped that the attitude taken by the government during the last session is not an indication of what the opposition is to expect during this parliament. In his speech on May 13, as recorded at page 35 of Hansard, the Prime Minister said:
Having done something to restore parliament in the measures which we have in mind-
And so on. I must say I am a little concerned about the measures the Prime Minister may have in mind. Of course there can be no question of not bringing down a regular budget this year, no matter how great a deficit the government may have incurred; and surely the measures the Prime Minister has in mind will continue to give parliament the right to have a debate on the budget, to scrutinize, to question and to vote on all the estimates of all the departments of government. As hon. members know, that was not done during the past session and hundreds of millions of dollars worth spent by governor general's warrants without bringing the estimates of the majority of the departments before the house, leaving an unprecedented gap in the budgetary history of our country. When the Prime Minister speaks of having done something to restore parliament, I wonder whether he has in mind the extraordinary procedure followed by the government in dissolving parliament last February. Those who were in the house or in the galleries that day will realize that there was much more stage setting and more theatri-calism than there was respect for the rights and traditions of parliament, or even fairness in the manner in which the house was dissolved.

Even Hansard could not record the atmosphere that was voluntarily built up around the dissolution of the house-the mystery surrounding the Prime Minister's flight to Quebec, the tension that was allowed to mount in the house from three o'clock on, the time when the Prime Minister arrived from Quebec, the photographers' flash bulbs as the Prime Minister entered the government lobby, his grand march into the House of Commons, the politically tinted valedictory speech he made at that time, and finally the solemn announcement that the members of parliament had been sitting for nothing because His Excellency the Governor General had already dissolved parliament.
Nor could Hansard record the vehement and justifiable protests of the leaders of the opposition groups against having been ruthlessly and unfairly cut off from saying one word in reply, contrary to all the customs and traditions of the house. Even Your Honour could not rule on the legality or fairness of the procedure that was followed in dissolving the house because there was no longer any House of Commons for Your Honour to preside over.
This type of procedure, I submit, may be interesting at Stratford on Avon and might even be justified and useful in a criminal court, but it has no place in the parliament of our country, and is all the more shocking coming from someone who such a very short time ago spoke so eloquently and so forcibly about the necessity of preserving the rights and dignity of this parliament. This incident, of course, did not win the election for the Conservatives and lose it for the Liberals. The Canadian public made their choice and I abide by it. But I feel certain that the people of Canada do not approve of and did not vote for government by tyranny or by drama, no matter how great majority they may have given the present government.
I also wonder, Mr. Speaker, whether the Prime Minister considered he was doing something to restore parliament in his recent attempt to ignore what has always been the accepted traditional and constitutional procedure of the house when dealing with international agreements of the importance of the NORAD pact which, as hon. members know, involves the stationing of Canadian troops abroad. Never before in the history of our country, and I am quite certain the Prime Minister was well aware of this, has Canada entered into an international agreement involving the stationing of Canadian troops abroad without introducing such an agreement in the house by way of a resolution and having the agreement ratified by parliament after a full and formal discussion

in the house; and this, Mr. Speaker, I submit, regardless of whether there was or was not unanimity on the particular agreement.
Never before has any prime minister seen fit to alter the customs and traditions followed by the house even on matters far less consequential than the NORAD pact simply because the prime minister presumed the opposition would be in favour of the agreement or because he considered the opposition not sufficiently strong or numerous to make a difference in the final outcome of the vote. As hon. members know the Prime Minister finally decided, after pressure was put on him by the Leader of the Opposition, to introduce the agreement by way of a resolution. We have just listened to the hon. member for Richelieu-Vercheres discuss unemployment in Canada. We are all aware of the unemployment situation which is existing in our country today, and there is no member of this house who is not kept constantly informed of conditions within his own riding, but unemployment is not just something which happens of itself. It has causes, and the logical way to deal with it is to search out those causes and try to cure them.

From the results of the election of March 31 there appears to be little doubt in the minds of the Canadian people that the blame for the situation does not belong at the feet of this government. Part of it, however, can be laid upon the fumbling and lack of action of the former Liberal administration, who were indifferent during their term of office to the wants of the Canadian people. We have experienced in this country a number of years of war-born prosperity, enhanced by the rapid development of our natural resources and new technological advances. During these years of easy prosperity our production costs, however, have risen faster than the prices we were receiving, and when the time arrived when we had to reduce our prices in order to make sales we found ourselves saddled with costs we were powerless to reduce. We seemed to have reached the stage at which the markets could no longer absorb our products at the prices we were asking. We had failed to reduce our costs; we had failed to reduce our prices, and we are failing to sell our products.
As our export sales have fallen off unemployment has increased among us. We cannot long continue to shut our eyes to the realities of the market and ask that our purchasing power be increased by increasing the number of dollars in circulation. The only way purchasing power can be increased is by increasing the production of those things which can be sold. In the final analysis it is the sale of goods with which we are concerned, for unless we export we perish economically.
Wage increases are of little value when we consider that all their advantage has been lost because they have caused higher living costs and prices and have brought about a slowing down of sales, increasing unemployment throughout the nation. This is a fact which must be impressed upon all union leaders as well as other classes within this nation, for there are many people in Canada who are unable to increase their incomes by means of union demands. I refer to the unorganized workers, the self-employed, the farmers, the fishermen, the lumbermen, those who are living on their savings and on their pensions. They, in addition to the unemployed, are the greatest sufferers from inflation caused by this continuous increase in wages. It is the responsibility of the government to assist these people wherever possible, and I wish to commend the government for extending the period during which unemployment insurance benefits are to be received. I submit, however, that one of the most important problems facing this government today is the problem of inflation. The incomes and savings of the majority of 57071-3-24i

I do not believe that Canada is today adrift in a fog. The plan for our future development is embodied in this throne speech for all to see. It outlines the plan for progress which is indicative of the vision of our Prime Minister and the present government. Plans are being made to accelerate the construction of useful public works and encourage the developing and processing of our vast natural resources. The government's plan to promote housing is commendable, for we know from past experience that this will be of great benefit to the manufacturing and building trades throughout the nation. This plan to further assist in the construction of new homes shows an awareness by the present government of the needs of many Canadian citizens.
Canada's population today is growing at an enormous rate, and this country is now in the world's most favourable position in terms of numbers of people and the resources with which to support them. I have the honour to represent the constituency of Queens-Lunenburg in Nova Scotia, which was at one time referred to as "down east". We do not hear this expression a great deal today, but in the days of wooden ships and iron men it was very common and being a down-easter set a man apart as one of the hardy breed who brought wealth and honour to our province and were responsible for many of the Canadian "firsts" belonging to Nova Scotia.
At Port Royal, for example, there was the first white settlement of Canada by the French, and at Halifax there was the first English town. Both the first Roman Catholic and Protestant churches were founded in Nova Scotia, as were the first grist mill, lighthouse, coal mine, law court, newspaper, dockyard and school. There Canada's first airplane flight was also made and the first drama to be written and staged, to name but a few.
With the passing of wooden ships as the most important means of travel, Nova Scotia did fall behind in the new era of industry and manufacture. A generation brought up in the tradition that our destiny was to carry a large part of the world's commerce appeared to be at a loss when the pattern changed. That was only a pause in our development, however, and throughout the whole province a new spirit of progress is awakening. We are looking ahead to see what we can do to make Nova Scotia a worthy home for the people who make up our families, our friends and our neighbours.
To this end I commend the government for outlining in the speech from the throne that unremitting efforts will be made to sell Canadian agricultural and fisheries products in the markets of the world. Our economy in Nova Scotia, and throughout the whole of the Atlantic provinces, is firmly based upon the fishing industry. It is the backbone of our foundries and shipyards and provides work for our wood lot owners who supply the shipyards with native wood for ship construction, as well as keeping a large number of our people employed in the shore fish processing plants.
Throughout my riding, from Mill Cove in Lunenburg county to St. Catherines river in Queens county, many of my people are directly engaged in deep sea or shore fishing. In Queens county the fishermen are mainly concerned with lobster fishing, while in

Lunenburg county the majority of the fishermen are engaged in deep sea or bank fishing. Due to the size of the Canadian population the bulk of the fresh fish catch, approximately 70 per cent, is sold on the United States market. The dried salt cod is still exported to traditional markets in the British West Indies, and in view of these facts all fishermen are deeply conscious of government effort to improve trade relations, not only with Great Britain but also with the United States. We in the Atlantic provinces must export our fish or we die economically.
Our market for salt codfish has now become the federation of the West Indies and this federation, faced with grave constitutional and financial problems, is looking to the new world for help. Their aim is to become a self-governing dominion within the commonwealth, but to do this they will need outside help along with hard work on the part of the some 3 million people of mixed origins in 10 British colonies made up of more than 15 islands in the Caribbean. While these islands are a mere 8,000 square miles of land, they are spread over a thousand-mile area of the Caribbean. The economies of these islands are similar and, outside of bauxite in Jamaica and oil in Trinidad, are based largely on exports of sugar, rum, bananas, citrus fruits and juices, cocoa, coffee, spices, copra and cotton.
In my opinion this new federation presents a challenge to Canada. Here is an opportunity to provide assistance to a people who are determined to take their place in the commonwealth, whose ideas of government coincide with ours, not communistic but democratic, with a parliament modelled after the British parliament. They must overcome terrific problems, for as separate British colonies these islands had erected customs and tariff barriers and also immigration bars against one another. These prevented the free flow of goods among the islands as well as preventing the citizens from moving freely from one island to the other. However, they are getting on with the job, and I commend the government for offering to donate a ship which will be built in Canada after the federation decides the type and size which will be most useful.
I would further suggest to the government that we investigate the possibility of increasing our imports from the new federation of bananas, citrus juices and dried citrus pulp, which is a valuable supplement in the feeding of beef and dairy cattle. Our imports of coffee and cocoa should also be stepped up, to say nothing about the traditional liquid we have imported into Nova Scotia for years.

This action on the part of Canada, will immediately provide the dollars needed to import from Canada potatoes, salt codfish and lumber, to name but a few of the items needed by a growing nation. This activity will stimulate our own economy, provide work for our people in the Atlantic provinces and again create industry in ports such as Liverpool and Port Medway in Queens county as well as the ports of Bridgewater and Lunenburg, where for years shiploads of lumber and fish were carried to the West Indies.
Speaking of fish, our great industry in the Atlantic provinces, I should like to refer to recent articles in the Halifax Herald and the Globe and Mail with regard to the quality at present exported to the West Indies. Complaints were registered by three members of the new West Indies government with regard to the price, quality and flavour of salt codfish presently obtained from Canada. Apparently there has been a decline in the quality of fish received from Canada, and some importers would like to obtain the high quality formerly received from Nova Scotia.
In my opinion the reason for this is the fact that Nova Scotia still uses the dory schooner in the catching of cod for the salt fish industry, though their numbers are declining; only 14 such vessels were in use during last year throughout the maritimes. Their numbers are declining because of inability to secure crews to go in fishing dories. However, it is an accepted fact that larger, better quality codfish are caught by hook and line than by the dragger method, as trawls can be set in areas where draggers cannot operate.
With this thought in mind, I believe encouragement should be given the industry by the government to combine the modern method of long lining, along with the schooner or mother ship. A schooner could accommodate on her deck four long liners, 40 feet in length, which could be loaded by the use of davits. The schooner would need to have a wider beam than usual to take care of the deck load, but this would increase her carrying capacity. The original cost of this combined operation would be rather excessive for private industry, but I believe the construction of a ship of this nature on a trial basis should be encouraged by the government with the hope of re-establishing the cod fishing, as well as strengthening the shipbuilding, industry and all allied industries by providing work in the shipyards of the maritimes.
I should like to say a few words at this time regarding the St. Lawrence seaway, on which I understand three-quarters of the work has been completed. This will cost the
The Address-Mr. Crouse Canadian people some $300 million, and I question whether this will ever be recovered within the 50-year recapture period or longer, regardless of the tolls charged. I should like to point out, however, the serious effects I believe this seaway will have upon our Canadian shipping industry. At the present time Canadian law permits ships of commonwealth registry to carry goods between Canadian ports. Under that privilege, ships of United Kingdom registry are rapidly taking over a growing share of Canada's domestic shipping business. In 1953 ships of United Kingdom registry carried five and one-half per cent of the traffic in the Canadian coastal trade, with 36 ships operating here. In 1954 they sent over 44 ships which carried seven and one-half per cent of the traffic, picking up an extra half million tons of cargo. In 1955 with 52 ships they picked up 10 per cent of the business with an increase of 1.2 million tons, and again in 1956 United Kingdom ships were up to 14 per cent of the traffic with 56 vessels carrying 2.3 million tons more than in 1955.
In 1956 United Kingdom flags carried all the iron ore moved up the St. Lawrence river from Seven Islands; 81 per cent of the coal from Cape Breton to St. Lawrence river ports, and much of the cargo shipped to sub-Arctic regions. The Canadian taxpayer pays part of the freight on Cape Breton coal moved inland under a policy of assisting the coal miner. He also pays much of the freight on cargo going to the Arctic, since it includes supplies used for defence and other government establishments. Yet, the majority of these shipping companies and their employees who move that freight pay no taxes in Canada. Unless this situation is changed it will be a matter of only a few years after the opening of the seaway, which is being built at such great cost to the Canadian taxpayer, until the Canadian coastal and inland lake and river fleet goes the same way as the Canadian deep sea fleet, which is out of business.
At the end of world war II we had the greatest merchant fleet per capita of any nation in the world. However, the former Liberal administration gave no thought to maintaining this fleet and sacrificed it through war assets disposal at prices in some instances below the cost of scraping the barnacles from the hulls. It is difficult today to rebuild this merchant fleet, for at the present prevailing scale of wages Canadian shipbuilders and coastal shipping operators simply cannot meet competition from the more cheaply built and operated United Kingdom ships.
In view of this situation I would urge the government that steps be taken now to reserve the Canadian coastal shipping business

The Address-Mr. Crouse to ships built and registered in Canada. In doing this Canada would be following the example of other highly industrialized countries, and I refer especially to the United States. This action would benefit our many shipyards and shipbuilders, not only in my riding and in the Atlantic provinces but throughout the greater part of Canada.
I should like to say a few words also at this time, Mr. Speaker, about the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This crown corporation has asked parliament to approve a total expenditure of $61,358,135 for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1959. This is an increase of $19,063,913 over last year, and in my opinion the time has arrived for a closer examination of the operations of this corporation which desires to spend so much of public funds.
I am not suggesting that there is any neglect, fraud or mishandling of public funds. However, I submit to you, sir, that the amounts presently required to produce strictly Canadian programs have become excessive when we consider that we are a nation of *only 17 million people. There is a limit 'beyond which conscience, or common sense, tells us we cannot go; and if we are to govern this nation on a sound, business-like basis, and continue to provide national radio and television service, I would earnestly suggest that this government place a maximum on expenditures of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
I repeat that $61,358,135 is too much money, by any yardstick to be spent on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Some of their productions are very good. Others, however, though lavish in the extreme are neither educational nor entertaining. I believe the expenditure by this corporation of $42,294,222 in 1957-58 to be ample and would request that the government give serious consideration to the reduction of this corporation's expenditures.
At this time I should also like to impress upon this house a matter of great interest to all Nova Scotians, especially those of my riding. I refer to the tourist industry. We have on the south shore of Nova Scotia the finest scenery to be found anywhere in Canada.

Good highways, excellent salt water bathing beaches at Sommerville, White Point and Crescent Beach to name but a few, the finest of lobster, scallops and other sea food served in cheerful surroundings, the finest of golf clubs and warm summer days and cool evenings offer to the tourist unexcelled opportunity for enjoyment. We are truly Canada's ocean playground, and the fact that the ferry Bluenose between

Yarmouth and Bar Harbor is filled to capacity each trip during the summer months is indicative of the number of Americans who have found this paradise of Nova Scotia and desire to visit and enjoy its beauty. There is ample evidence that the Bluenose alone is unable to cope with the demand for accommodation, and this summer a United States company is also planning to operate a steamship service between Boston and Yarmouth.
This is the age of travel, and in my opinion this demand from the travelling public could well be met by the construction of a second ferry which would provide a continuous service between Boston and Shelburne, Nova Scotia. I make the suggestion because there is no assurance that the United States company will provide its service beyond 1958, and I believe this expansion of tourist facilities could be considered on the basis of federal assistance programs provided in other fields of national development elsewhere in Canada. When making my maiden speech on November 13 last I expressed this opinion, and I wish to again impress upon the government the need of establishing this additional service along the south shore.
In closing I wish to state that the people of Queens-Lunenburg still have many unsolved problems. We have our share of unemployment and difficulty in marketing our pulpwood. Our shipyards are not as busy as in former years, and the prices for fish to our fishermen have not shown a noticeable increase in the last ten years. Our farmers share the same marketing problems experienced by farmers throughout other parts of Canada. However, our people were definitely influenced and impressed by the program of the Conservative party. They were convinced that here was a truly national policy which would take cognizance of the special problems of the maritimes and of the province of Nova Scotia. I believe that as these policies are implemented we will begin to grow and develop and continue to make in the future, as in the past, our contribution to the national economy of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I along with so many other hon. members offer to you, to the Deputy Speaker and to the deputy chairman of committees my very best wishes and congratulations. The people of Canada, in the light of the composition of this house, and in the light of some rather difficult situations we encountered in the past and which we may face in the years ahead, are at this time looking forward with a great deal of confidence to our Speakers of the House of Commons for the maintenance of the traditional rights and privileges of every individual hon. member of this house.
My opening remarks in this debate are an expression of gratitude to the electors of my riding for once again choosing me as their representative. Unlike the hon. member for Charlotte I do not propose to say anything adverse about any of my opponents in the election campaign just completed, or indeed in any other election campaign. Perhaps it is because I come from British Columbia that I am able to say any opponent I have ever had in an election campaign, had he been elected to this house, would have served to the utmost of his or her ability. I always recognize that their intentions in offering their services were just as sincere as mine.
I feel gratitude to the people of my riding in a greater degree than ever before in view of the great emotional wave that seemed to sweep across the country on March 31. Indeed, many of us on April 1 had the feeling that a hurricane has passed over leaving only a few shorn lambs. Nevertheless the harsh realities of the economic uncertainties which are becoming evident in every aspect of our economic structure, including the harsh reality of unemployment, are like cold winds causing a new growth of wool to appear on our backs, and before very long I am sure the people of Canada will be convinced again that they have in this parliament opposition members who are so essential to good government.
I do not feel it desirable to rehash the election campaign just concluded. The decision has been made and I offer my congratulations to the Prime Minister on his accomplishment. Perhaps I should also extend congratulations to the advertising agency that was employed during the course of the campaign. However, for the sake of all of us I wish him and his government well.
The Address-Mr. Regier I believe it is vital that an opposition member always place the welfare of the Canadian people ahead of the welfare of his political group, regardless of how keenly he may feel that he and his political movement have all the answers. I think it may be fairly said of the C.C.F. movement that while adhering firmly over the years to their fundamental principles its members have always expressed acceptance of the ultimate wisdom of the people. The evolution of our society has for centuries rested on the people making progress by means of trial and error. The very essence of democratic socialism is a faith in man's ability-yes, even in his responsibility-to rule himself, and we propose that man ought to rule himself in the economic field as well. Therein lies the basic reason for our denunciation of the principle involved in the rule of either the dictates of capital or the dictates of a political machine.
Having said that may I say, Mr. Speaker, that we also oppose government by the dictation of an individual regardless of who he is, what he has accomplished or whatever ability he may have. At this point I should like, in all seriousness, to utter a word of warning. I do not believe that either personal or public interest is served by the tendency of the present Prime Minister to decide it all and to do it all. Inasmuch as some 23 Conservatives have now been admitted as members of Her Majesty's privy council, surely that ought to confer upon each of them a measure of responsibility and authority, and should mean a little more than merely being obliged to be the parrot or mouthpiece of someone else's thinking.
When the Prime Minister was in the opposition first as the member for Lake Centre and later as the member for Prince Albert he used to be very outspoken in his condemnation of what he regarded as the sins of the Liberal government, in that he claimed that they were violating the rights of parliament, the traditional forms and institutions, and were lacking in respect for the crown. I hold in my hand some of the Prime Minister's election campaign literature. I believe this particular piece was delivered to hundreds of thousands of homes throughout the country. Under the heading "Man of Action" is a picture of what is supposed to be "The Diefenbaker cabinet". It is of some significance that Her Majesty's privy council in Canada is now called the Diefenbaker cabinet. However, that may be understandable in the heat of an election campaign. But of even greater significance to me is the insult to the crown, in that in the centre of the picture of the Diefenbaker cabinet I see a

The Address-Mr. Regier photograph of His Excellency the Governor General, supposedly a member of that cabinet.
Senior members of parliament can well imagine what the former member for Lake Centre and Prince Albert, now the Prime Minister, would have said in the house had any other political party ever had the nerve to include the Governor General as a member of a particular cabinet. I know, Mr. Speaker, that according to the rules of the house the political leanings of the Governor General are not a subject of debate in the house. Therefore I cannot pursue the matter further at this time, beyond expressing the hope that I trust the Governor General will never become a member of anybody's cabinet, not even a member of the Diefenbaker cabinet.
The survival of our society, Mr. Speaker, without the continuation of the suicidal armaments race is, I believe, a subject of paramount importance to the Canadian people at the present time. There seems to be an air of utter frustration. We seem to be at a loss with respect to where to go from here. Those on each side of the iron curtain are devoting so much of their energies not to the promotion of life, not to the promotion of happiness, but to the building of ever more horrible weapons of mass destruction. We are doing this in the light of the lessons of history, which surely show that an armament race has always ended in war and disaster. The disaster that would be caused by a war at this time would be beyond compare in history.
We hate to think of the vast sums of money that we and our allies are devoting to the armament race. In fact when we consider the economies of some of our European allies, notably Italy and France, we begin to wonder whether we are not hurting them possibly even more than we are helping them, in that the armament race is forcing their economies to the verge of bankruptcy. The western world will find that its money has been very poorly invested indeed if in elections in Italy or France the people should elect communist governments. Our whole concept of western defence would then fall apart like a house of cards. In the opinion of many people we have reached a point where we ought to give this matter very serious consideration indeed.
Added to this, Mr. Speaker, are the warnings issued on many occasions by an ever growing number of leading world scientists about the danger of nuclear experiments and explosions, and the possibility exists that even now we are doing more injury to the human race by these experiments than any wa' has ever inflicted upon mankind.

The battle for the survival of our society is being waged on three fronts, the military preparedness phase, the economic phase and the psychological phase. We have apparently reached a stalemate in the armament race, since either side has enough nuclear weapons at its disposal to blow the whole world to pieces. Why they want to go on manufacturing any more I do not know, unless they have evil designs on other worlds. We are not sure which side is ahead in the armament race. However, on the economic and phycho-logical fronts we are becoming convinced that we are behind, that month by month we are losing the race.
We seem to be unwilling to engage in any kind of peaceful competition with the Soviet world. I submit that the reason we are unwilling to engage in peaceful competition with the Soviet world is that this would involve our government assuming a responsibility which we in this group feel it ought to assume, while those in office are unwilling to have the government involved in that responsibility. We contend that if we are sincere in our expressions of belief that free men are able under a freely elected government to offer more to the people than can be offered under a totalitarian government, we should be able to produce results for our people superior to those a totalitarian government is able to offer to its people. I often believe there may be a lack of basic faith in the ability of a free government in a free society to offer more to the people than can be offered by a totalitarian government.
Surely the solution is not a continuation of the already overly dangerous armament race. Surely the solution is a new kind of competition. By all means let us have competition with the Soviet world, but let it be competition to prove to ourselves and to the rest of the world that our type of society is in fact superior. Our finest line of defence, and I believe our only real line of defence, is to prove that we have more to offer, that we are able to do more.
There are others in the world who are not yet committed to our way of life or to the way of life of the totalitarian regimes. These hundreds of millions of others in the world are watching us. I am referring here to the psychological war. These people are watching what we do. They are watching what we are able to offer. I feel it is our lack of faith in our ability to do more than we are doing that is causing us to lose that psychological war.
When those who are watching realize that we had according to the latest dominion bureau of statistics bulletin of May 21, 506,000 people without work in April or 8.6 per cent

of our labour force, and another 501,000 or 8.4 per cent of our labour force who worked less than 35 hours a week, how will they feel? What will they think when they read, as I read, that the Minister of Finance on April 21 admitted in his speech in Hamilton, Ontario, that by the end of 1957 unemployment as a percentage of the labour force was higher than at any time in the post-war period. Under the influence of seasonal factors it continued to rise until about the middle of last month, March, he said.
I wish we could have had that type of realism, an admission of that situation from the Minister of Finance, before the last parliament was dissolved on February 1. At that time, however, we were told not to worry; everything would be all right. In fact, as late as March 12 the Prime Minister, speaking in Exhibition Gardens in Vancouver, thundered to the audience of thousands that despite the statistic-I am paraphrasing his words-"I can assure you we are past the peak". He demanded that the people of Canada have faith in his words. Yet at the end of April we have the Minister of Finance telling us that the Prime Minister was a little less than honest in insisting that the people take his word that we were past the peak.
I am not blaming this government alone for the conditions we have today. The immediate post-war period released a great pent-up demand for consumer goods. This demand resulted in a terrific expansion of our productive capacity in Canada, even at times at the cost of our social needs. We in this group were continually warning the government if necessary to limit this fantastic expansion of our productive capacity in order that our social needs might also be met. However, not much attention was paid to us, and there was this headlong expansion. We had this delayed consumer demand accompanied by the removal of price controls at far too early a date by governments that were willing to appease the selfish desires of those who saw huge profits available to them if they could satisfy these demands and charge all that the traffic would bear.
At that time we began to lose our foreign markets. We failed to extend sufficient credits overseas. We stubbornly refused to accept soft currency until we forced the soft currency nations of the free world to learn to get along without us. They have been doing very well by themselves. This is not the result of their desire but the result of our stubborn refusal to accept soft currency or to extend to them the helping hand which they needed so badly at that time. It is absolutely of our making that there is in existence what is known as the European
The Address-Mr. Regier common market. It was the United States and Canada who were primarily responsible for the countries of Europe knitting their economies more closely together and learning how to get along without Canadian products. We insisted on relying on the United States for our markets, failing to realize that the United States was a market for us only at such times as there was great expansion within that country and they had urgent need of our surplus production. We blandlj refused to do any business with many areas of the world. Even today we refuse to see one-fourth of the people of the world- naturally I refer to the people living in China-and to share responsibility for those in dire need.
We have refused to recognize the growing awareness of our standards of people in other parts of the world, or their desire to attain our standards of living. We refuse to recognize their knowledge that they do not have to continue living on the brink of starvation as their forefathers did for centuries. Once again I must express my appreciation of the honesty of the Minister of Finance. When he spoke in Waterloo on May 15 he made reference to our extended productivity. He said:
The net effect of all this has been that, between 1946 and 1956, productivity per man-year in the private sector of the economy has risen by nearly three per cent annually. The percentage has, of course, varied from year to year. Last year appears to have been somewhat out of line in this regard, but the long-run trend is nonetheless upward.
If it was 3 per cent per year for a ten-year period, that means an increase of upwards of 30 per cent in our productivity, according to the figures given by the minister. Then later on he said:
If account is taken of the increased population, per capita real income has risen by about 10 per cent since 1947, most of the rise occurring since 1950.
In other words, labour has raised its productivity by upwards of 30 per cent in a ten-year period, while the purchasing power of labour has been allowed to grow by only about 10 per cent. Karl Marx himself could not have made a finer analysis than the Minister of Finance did when he spoke in Waterloo. We rob our workers and farmers of their purchasing power by denying them the benefit of their increased productivity. This lost the domestic market for us. Yes, for a time we were able to carry on because we extended credit in the consumer field. The finance companies waxed rich. We offered goods with no downpayment. However, everything comes to an end, and the day has arrived when the average workingman owes so much he cannot add to his monthly payment burden. As a result we have a decline in his purchasing power.

The Address-Mr. Regier
Added to that we have had high interest rates charged by these companies and others which have robbed the people of purchasing power. We have had the growing taxation on homes and incomes, with no rehef over many years. We have had a shortchanging of the short-term small investor by huge corporations, in that they receive less than the corporation net earnings when corporations often keep over half the net earnings in the business to the benefit, I will admit, of the long-term investor but certainly at the expense of the short-term investor. This small investor is often supposed to be the real owner of Canada, although he is not.
There are many reasons that can be cited as the causes of our depression. However, no solution is being offered at the present time by the government in office. The government with its speech from the throne reminds me of the man with the inner tube. It is an old inner tube with many holes in it that have been patched over the years. All that our present Prime Minister had to offer in this election campaign, when the air was coming out of the inner tube at a dozen different places, was this. He simply had a bigger box of new patches than had the Liberals. In our opinion what is needed is a new inner tube, because the old inner tube has patch beside patch and our whole economic system is being kept alive by putting on more patches; and our speeches from the throne, with little patches here and little patches there, are therefore tending to grow longer and longer.
The only other remedy is that of deficit financing. I hope the government realizes the inflationary danger of deficit financing. Deficit financing at a time of deflation can serve a useful purpose indeed, but at a time when we have recession combined with inflation, deficit financing could wreak havoc to the economy of the country.
As to the Liberal amendment, we intend to support it; I am inclined to agree with it. I see nothing wrong with more trade. But I read carefully the speech of the Leader of the Opposition and I notice that he failed to offer one single way in which this government might increase its trade. The Liberal leader calls for increased trade but he does not say how it should be increased.
The whole system, Mr. Speaker, is rapidly breaking down. I find no less an authority for this than again the Minister of Finance. It is amazing how frank the Conservative government can become once it is firmly in the saddle. Some of us remember only too well how brutally frank the last Conservative government was in the years from 1930 to


1935. However, in Waterloo the Minister of Finance had this to say:
One of the charges which are levelled against free enterprise is that it admits of times of economic instability. There may, of course, be a grain of truth in this, . . .
Those are the words of the Minister of Finance, and it is our contention that there is a great deal more than a grain of truth in them. If it is only a grain it must be a mustard seed, indeed which is assuming alarming proportions.
We are often asked the question, "What would you do about unemployment?" I think part of the answer is in our subamendment. We realize that it is good for our country to increase international trade. However, we contend that the main market for the products of Canadian labour and Canadian farmers is right at home. It is for that reason that my house leader submitted his amendment to the Liberal amendment. Increased foreign trade is not enough. Our first responsibility is to our Canadian people. On the home front lies our major solution.
While recognizing the importance of trade with other countries, we have advocated that Canada be prepared to spend as much as 1 per cent of our gross national production in order to win friends for democracy throughout the world, and in order to enhance the prospect of Canadian trade as well. We have advocated the extension of credits, the acceptance in part payment at least of soft currency. I believe we should seriously attempt to align ourselves with the European common market.
I am greatly interested in the Liberal member's resolution on the order paper calling for free trade with the federation of the British West Indies. I note with a great deal of pleasure that the organized labour movement is doing much, through the international confederation of free trade unions, to raise living standards in other areas of the world to the end that the workers of foreign countries shall have an equally high standard of living compared with workers in Canada, and not be able to offer the unfair competition on world markets that is being offered. We have advocated export and import boards and an end to this farce of high tariffs and low tariffs, which to the people of Canada always means high tariffs in effect, regardless of what government is in office.
On the home front we have called for a national investment board so there shall be an even development of the Canadian economy, so that our social needs will be met along with the need to increase our productivity. We have asked for a curtailment of the activities of huge corporations. I see

no reason why we should not be reimposing an excess profits tax in Canada. I feel that no corporation in Canada should be allowed to earn more than 12 per cent on its net capital investment. We have hundreds of thousands of small independent enterprisers and businessmen who would be most happy indeed if they were able to earn 12 per cent per annum on their net investment.
We hear the argument made that they are not making this money. I was greatly interested in this release put out by the united steel workers of America. I have never yet heard anyone say their research department turned out fictitious figures. I believe they are reliable. I note that the five major steel companies of Canada in 1947 had a net income of $28,600,000, and that in 1956 this figure had grown to $142,300,000. In 1947 they received as net income 13.2 per cent of every sales dollar. In 1956 they received as net income 20.9 per cent of each and every sales dollar. These corporations are well able to afford the wages they are paying and in many cases they are able to afford a good deal more. Some of them are also able to afford a reduction in prices which the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg mentioned as being necessary.
We call for a vastly expanded program of welfare measures, higher pensions for our retired civil servants, for our retired railroad men, retired members of the R.C.M.P. and a fairer deal for veterans. The government still has restored to the veterans only one-half of the buying power they have lost through inflation. We call for a national health insurance program.
I know the old song and story that you are going to bankrupt the country, that the country cannot afford these things. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska call for higher family allowances the other day. I see, Mr. Speaker, that last year the people of Canada spent over $1,000 million on liquor. If they can spend $61 per capita per annum on liquor they can spend a little more than that on either education or health and welfare. I am absolutely unwilling to accept any argument that the Canadian economy cannot afford decent allowances for senior citizens, for our veterans, for our retired people and for those who are attempting to bring up families.
How long can we afford to operate in our country allowing each branch of industrial enterprise to organize in its own selfish interests without necessarily having any regard for the public welfare? We say the time has come when the people must use the instrument of government to plan their economic welfare. The situation in the world
The Address-Mr. M. Smith is grave indeed, and it affects all mankind. We must with determination resolve our course for our very survival. We have to prove to our people and to others that democracy is worth while. The highest appeals and platitudes will not survive the harsh, cold and cruel realities which dictate the actions of both capital and labour at the present time. If we have the courage to end the exploitation of man by man, if we are aware of our responsibilities and if we will have faith in ourselves and in our people, then the weapon of government will preserve the heritage of the past and may also be used as a mighty instrument for the building of a new society, a society that will make for peace in the world and will make health and happiness for the Canadian people a reality.

Mr. Speaker, may I begin by adding my congratulations to the many which Your Honour and your deputy have received. I should also like to congratulate my friends the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. La-freniere) and the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen), who so capably moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I have the privilege of sharing my office space-although he says it is his office space-with the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency, who is also acting as my French tutor, and be informs me that my French is so bad that I had better not attempt to use it today.
This is a memorable moment, but one that makes me, like most new members, nervous. It is a happy moment for me, yet at the same time to some extent it is a sad one, by reason of the fact that one of my best friends and one of the best friends of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) did not live to see this day. He worked tirelessly for us during the election campaign in June and worked with us in succeeding months in establishing an organization for our future success. The members from Manitoba and the public of Manitoba will know the name Alf Francis when they hear it.
Not since 1921 has a Conservative member of parliament been able to bring greetings from the citizens of Winnipeg North to this house, and I trust that hon. members in the corner to my right will grasp the significance of this statement, and after relating it to certain statements by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. MacLean) will have a clearer picture of what might lie in the future.
With the indulgence of the house I would like very briefly to tell you, Mr. Speaker, about the constituency of Winnipeg North.

Smith It includes the north part of the city of Winnipeg as well as that part of Winnipeg known as Elmwood; it also includes the city of East Kildonan, a city of some 20,000 citizens, and West Kildonan, an area which is rapidly approaching the size of a city. Before I proceed I would like to refer to a couple of statements made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate who spoke yesterday afternoon. He mentioned that he thought most of the voters in Canada were blinded by the vision. I would like to assure him that such was not the case in Winnipeg North. Many voters in my constituency were not born in Canada, and it is quite likely that certain statements made by the former Liberal minister of citizenship and immigration had a great deal of influence in their voting.
