speechtext:
It has been said that the speech from the throne is one of the best ever presented to this house, and I am certain that the citizens of Winnipeg North will heartily concur in this statement. Many of them will derive benefit from the extension of the unemployment insurance benefits, and many more will benefit from the increased funds available under the National Housing Act.
Many of the people in my constituency have been requesting a bill of rights, and the small businessmen will certainly be glad to hear of the small business section to be established within the administrative machinery of government. The opposition in


this house may say what it pleases, but many of the items contained in the speech from the throne are things which the people of Winnipeg North have wanted for some time, and they realized that the only way to get them was to put a Conservative government in power in Ottawa.
I would now like to heartily endorse what my hon. friend the member for Winnipeg North Centre advocated with regard to those persons who have physical disabilities and handicaps. His remarks in this regard may be found at page 222 of Hansard for May 19 last. I was very privileged to have several physically handicapped people on my campaign committee. I know they do not want charity; all they want is a chance to show that they can do as good a job as anyone else. I strongly urge this government, therefore, to consider employing a physically handicapped person in every employment office, whose duty it would be to find jobs for others who are physically handicapped.
During the election campaign prior to June 10, a campaign in which as a newcomer my committee firmly entrenched me in third place, just a mere 13,500 votes behind the winner, I found that many people in Winnipeg North were keenly interested in the field of education.
In November last, when the Soviet union successfully launched two earth satellites, this interest increased tremendously, as it did, I am sure, in the whole world. This interest has not yet subsided in Winnipeg North, for it was one of the main subjects I encountered during the election campaign. Therefore as the representative of some 60,000 electors, the majority of whom are interested in education, and as a member of parliament well under 30 years of age and hence not long out of university, I feel I should speak for a few moments on the subject of education.
I do not propose to give advice to educators, for one of my former professors occupies a seat on the other government side of the house, nor do I propose to give advice to students. But I do propose to make a few suggestions to the government with regard to this matter. I have observed that a few hon. members have spoken on this important subject, and I trust that the opinions of others will be forthcoming either during this debate or on another occasion.
In order to realize the importance of education in our society today, one needs only to look at the tremendous and almost unbelievable advances which have been made in the last few years in one small part of this field, namely the field of science. Man, through his unquenchable thirst for knowledge, has brought the threshold of space before us. He

has brought it together with such exciting and, as yet, almost incomprehensible ideas as space travel which are only a moment away in this eternity of time. He has introduced, too, the shattering prospect of a global nuclear war which could result in the extermination of all forms of life from the earth or the obliteration of our planet from the universe. A vast amount of knowledge and research has been required to bring us this far, and an even greater amount will be required to take us further.
What are other governments of the world doing about education? First let us look at the U.S.S.R., the power which at the moment appears to lead the world in certain technological aspects and which, therefore, must lead the world in education in those aspects. In Russia education is still controlled by the government. It is regimented education. I do not propose for one moment that this government or any provincial government should tell our youth what to learn and how to learn it, but it is interesting to compare education in the U.S.S.R. with education in other countries. Indeed, the government of the United States is already doing this. President Eisenhower has made several telecasts on this matter, telecasts that were carried in Canada. Also, the Prudential Insurance Company produced a lengthy program entitled, "Where Do We Stand?", which compared at length the two educational systems together with the curricula and results.
Periodicals are also making comparisons. I hold in my hand a number of publications containing articles comparing or dealing with the two systems. First is an article in the December 6, 1957 edition of V.S. News and World Report. It is entitled "A Size-Up of What's Wrong With the American Schools" and is written by Rear Admiral H. H. Rick-over, of the United States navy. The second is an article entitled "Education in the U.S.S.R.", which appears in the January, 1958 edition of School Life, published by the United States government. The third publication, The Reporter, is a New York publication and I refer to a contribution in the February 20, 1958 edition in which there are two articles: first, "Are Soviet Schools Better Than Ours?" and second, "A Scientist's Impressions of Russian Research". The fourth publication is the March, 1958 edition of Reader's Digest, which contains an article entitled, "Russia Rings the School Bell", which is condensed from "Inside Russia Today", written by John Gunther. Life magazine for March 24, 1958 contains "a vital new series", as they call it, entitled "Crisis In Education" which contains exclusive pictures of a Russian schoolboy and his United States counterpart.
The Address-Mr. M. Smith
To return, Mr. Speaker, to the book entitled "Education in the U.S.S.R.", this book was published in 1957 by the United States government and is a complete study of Soviet education up to the time of the Soviet economical reorganization initiated in May, 1957. I should like to place certain parts of this work on the record to show the details into which the study goes. At page 67 the study deals with "Curriculum". Paragraph 4 on that page reads as follows:
Whereas the Soviet students graduating from secondary schools in June, 1955 had taken courses in physics for five years, astronomy for one year, chemistry for four years, biology for five years and mathematics including arithmetic, algebra, geometry, and trigonometry, for 10 years, less than a third of the American high school graduates had taken a year of chemistry, about a fourth had had a year of physics, and less than a seventh had taken advanced mathematics.
At page 74 the second paragraph, under the heading of "Arithmetic and Mathematics", reads as follows:
The arithmetic cycle is completed with grade V, which includes fractions, decimals, percentages and proportions. Slide rules and arithmometers are introduced at this time. Algebra and geometry begin in grade VI, continue in grade VII, and are studied in some detail in subsequent grades.
The next paragraph reads as follows:
Mathematics courses continue with algebra and geometry through grade X, and with trigonometry and an introduction to calculus in grades IX and X.
At page 81 under the heading "Physics", the first paragraph reads as follows:
Physics, introduced in grade VI, relates to the rudiments of mechanics and hydrodynamics. In grade VII the branches dealing with heat, light and electricity are introduced. The teaching of physics includes demonstration and experimentation.
The next paragraph reads as follows:
Physics courses continue with a more detailed and systematic study of mechanics-kinematics, dynamics and statics-heat, light and electricity in grade VIII; molecular physics and heat in grade IX; and electricity, optics and sound or aerodynamics in grade X. The amount of required laboratory work is considerably increased.
On page 82 under the heading "Chemistry", we find the following:
Chemistry is started in grade VII, with a short outline of the main chemical conceptions-substances, elements, atomic-molecular structure, oxides, salts, laws of weight preservation, plus a study of oxygen, hydrogen, air and water. Demonstration and experimentation accompany the course. A systematic presentation of inorganic chemistry is required in grades VIII and IX, and an introduction to organic chemistry in grade X.
On page 89 under the heading "Homework", we find:
In 1952 a special decree, was issued setting maximum limits for the amount of homework a Soviet pupil might be assigned as follows: for pupils in grade I, net more than one hour a day; grade II, between one and one and one-half hours; in grades III and IV, up to two hours; in grades V and VI,
374	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. M. Smith from two to three hours; in grade VII, from two and one-half to three and one-half hours; and in grades VIII to X, from three to four hours a day.
The study deals also with such questions as schools tor adults, schools tor working youth, evening schools tor rural youth, schools tor the mentally retarded, blind, deaf or hard of hearing, physical rehabilitation, schools for the exceptionally bright, schools for the artistically gifted, and military and naval schools. It also goes into details on extracurricular work and activities, vocational training, semi-professional training, teacher training, and so on.
I would strongly urge each hon. member of this house who is interested in education to read this publication and the articles I have mentioned. I do not for a moment suggest that we in Canada should follow the system which is now being used in the Soviet union, but it is my belief that the government of this country could do more for education than it is doing at present. As a matter of fact, educational activity in Russia may be beneficial to the whole world, for once people learn to think it is difficult to prevent them from going further. It is quite possible that the processes in operation in Russia will produce in time a democratic government in that country.
I realize that education is primarily a provincial matter, but as I have suggested I believe the federal government can do more for education than it has done in the past. I suggest that the government set up a committee on education. The committee could be a cabinet committee or it could be a committee in the Department of National Health and Welfare. It could even be a committee similar to the one to be set up with regard to small business.
This committee would not in any way interfere with provincial jurisdiction over education; I want to make that quite clear. I would suggest, however, that it could perform some of the following services. It could act as an information centre and do unlimited research in the field of education. It could investigate and report on education in each province of Canada and in some other countries of the world, including the United States or Russia. It could make public its findings and the facts it gleaned from its investigations. Those publications could be made available to the public at large and especially to the ministers of education in the various provinces.
It could be a committee that could be approached by universities with regarding to seeking financial aid. It could be a committee approachable by students when seeking tax cuts or relief from the payment of unemployment insurance. It could seek the


co-operation of the press and the home. I believe the press can play a highly important part in the field of education. If the press devoted as much coverage to the success of students who graduate from universities as it does to students who participate in sports we might find an increased incentive on the part of our students in the universities, with the result that we would produce more trained scientists than we are now producing.
Education is becoming more complicated and costly every day. One could go on to discuss the cost of building schools, the cost of equipment for laboratories, the salaries of professors and so on. But one must also realize that education is much more than what I have mentioned here. I have dwelt primarily on scientific study, but we could devote much time to a discussion of the arts and humanities. I do not pretend to be an expert on education, but in our democracy even the man in the street has a right to express his views, and for a member of this house it is his duty.
I sincerely hope that I have succeeded today in igniting a spark that will be fanned by the opinions of others until together we will have succeeded in lighting a fire that will brighten the hopes and ambitions of everyone who seeks to better himself in any way whatsoever by that process which we call education.

speakeroldname: Mr. C. R. Granger (Grand Falls-White Bay-Labrador):
subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should imagine that every new member approaches the duty of delivering his first speech in this chamber with timidity and uneasiness. Unless he were a complete extrovert he would have a feeling of reserve and modesty when he remembers how many men of unquestioned ability and experience have been in this house for many years. But I take comfort from the thought that experience and wisdom almost invariably breed tolerance, and I have no doubt but that I will receive a sympathetic and even kindly hearing, and if I should unwittingly essay to be profound I am sure I will be forgiven even if there are some inward smiles.
I wish to join with those hon. members who have extended to the Speaker congratulations on his appointment to his high office. I share with them the conviction that he will discharge his duties with fairness and add to the dignity of this chamber. I would also like to congratulate the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Crouse) on his speech. I agreed with much of what he said, particularly his remarks concerning fish markets and the West Indies.
I would now like to say a word about the great riding which I have the honour to

represent. To do so is natural, I suppose, but in this case my remarks will be all the more effective because I speak with sincere pride in praise of my riding. Not only is it one of the largest ridings in our nation, but in terms of importance and variety it is one of the greatest areas in North America. From Grand Falls and Gander in the south, all through the district of Green Bay, White Bay south, White Bay north, Labrador south and Labrador north it stretches on to cape Chidley in the far north. It embraces the industrial centres of Newfoundland with their great pulp and paper industry and woods operations, the famous international airport at Gander, the traditional fisheries of Green Bay, White Bay and the Labrador coast, the great military airport at Goose, one of the great bastions of western defence, and the mines and timber and untouched resources and undreamed of wealth of the new and magic world of Labrador.
It is a great riding, larger than many nations, almost as big as some continents, with some of the finest people who can be found anywhere, citizens of whom Canada may be proud. A tradition in which courage and toil are commonplace have bred a race of people whose loyalty and dependability are beyond question. I think it is only right that I should mention the industries which are vital to these people, and some of the things they require.
Most of the people in my riding are fishermen and loggers; and the fisheries, the traditional industry of Newfoundland, are still of paramount importance. Up to the time of confederation the Newfoundland fisheries continued in much the same manner as they had for hundreds of years. It is true that since John Cabot's discovery of Newfoundland in 1497 the cod trap and the gasoline marine engine were invented, but by and large the system remained virtually unchanged. It is also true that the fresh fish business enjoyed a vigorous start prior to confederation, but this new industry was due for tremendous expansion at the same time that the salt cod fishery was to undergo a revolution, for after confederation the fisheries of Newfoundland underwent a great change.
This was due to three factors. I give them not necessarily in the order of importance, for no one can assess which made the greatest contribution, but with confederation several things happened to this ancient industry. In the first instance the return of democratic rule in Newfoundland, as it does everywhere in the world, released energies which heretofore had been restricted, and the combination of self-government, free enterprise and competitive operation opened new vistas for
The Address-Mr. Granger merchants and fishermen alike. Then the federal Department of Fisheries brought to the fisheries of Newfoundland its experience, technical knowledge and the funds with which to experiment, which gave us the laboratory plant always so badly needed, while the provincial government under Premier Smallwood embarked on a wise and bold policy of supplying financial assistance to firms which desired to expand. The result was an expansion in the industrialization of fisheries in eight years unequalled during the preceding four and one-half centuries.
However, unfortunately for the people of my riding the expansion has been largely to the south, its northern position thus far having precluded it from enjoying much of the benefits of modern progress, although some progress has been made.
It may be that this is a geographical handicap and a difficult one to overcome but simply because it is difficult is no reason for it to be forgotten.
One of the great natural resources of Canada is fishing and the waters of northern Newfoundland and Labrador are rich with fish. When John Cabot sailed west he was after gold and precious jewels. He did not find them in Newfoundland but he did find waters teeming with fish which proved to be better than precious metals. I know that Canada has undeveloped resources other than those in the waters of Newfoundland and I realize that these other resources require attention, but I do think it wrong that any great resource should be neglected and despite all that has been done we have merely touched the fringes.
If Canada is to be really great all of her resources must be developed, but the inroads made in our fishery markets by foreign competitors and the multitude of craft flying strange flags in Newfoundland waters today make me wonder if, while gaining wealth on the one hand we are not throwing it away with the other. I am not suggesting that the stranger be deprived of fishing rights but I am suggesting that our way of doing business be so improved as to make it economically undesirable for him to do so. I therefore ask that more serious attention than ever be given to the development, expansion and exploitation of the wealth which lies in Canadian waters. The oldest part of our heritage has been one of our richest and the fishing business can be improved so that it will provide an attractive vocation for our people and so that the fishermen will be not only a valuable man but a well paid man.
One immediate need in northern Newfoundland is more adequate bait supplies, more bait depots and a better distribution

The Address-Mr. Granger agency. This is something that can be done immediately and I hope that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) has plans in this direction for early implementation.
I have referred earlier to the two great airports which are in my riding. Goose is another military airport and is used extensively by the United States air force as well as the R.C.A.F. There is little that I should say here except to make one or two observations. First, I should like to see a higher proportion of Newfoundlanders employed at Goose airport, particularly on construction work. Second, I think it only fair that the town of Happy Valley, where so many of our permanent workers at Goose Bay live, should be allowed to obtain its electricity from the R.C.A.F. plant at Goose. A public wharf at Happy Valley is badly needed but I shall speak of that and other marine works at a more appropriate time. Suffice it to say here that Goose is one of the most important military airports in the western world. Few either know or realize its value but it is one of the great defence fortresses of this age.
Gander, of course, is one of the famous airports of the world. In this air age it is the great gateway to Canada. It is the only part of Canada which millions of visitors ever see. In this rapidly moving twentieth century it already has a long history. The history of Gander is the history of modern aviation. Very few of us have ever had the proper appreciation of Gander's value to the pioneering period of yesterday or its great commercial value today. I think I will be forgiven if I should stress a little here just how important Gander was both to the world of aviation and to Canada in particular. Prior to confederation, at the international conferences in Geneva when routes and landing stations on both sides of the Atlantic were being arranged, it was toward the Newfoundland representative that most attention was directed because Newfoundland, having both Gander and Goose, held the key to the whole over-all strategy. Newfoundland's position was extremely important and her bargaining power was tremendous.
Prior to confederation I believe Canada's representatives at those international conferences attended as observers only. I believe in those days Canada had been unable to receive permission to fly commercial planes over United States territory which would sit down and pick up passengers in competition with United States planes. However, confederation gave Canada the key that unlocked all these doors. The acquisition of Gander by Canada increased her bargaining power so that she was able to negotiate from strength and from then on she was quickly

able to obtain landing rights in almost every part of the world except Russia. Canada was suddenly transformed into one of the great forces in modern commercial aviation. The impact of this change in Canadian civil air power must have had a tremendous economic effect, the results of which must have been very favourable to the whole Canadian economy. Certainly with Canadian planes carrying the Canadian flag into far distant places Canada was receiving the best and most potent advertising possible.
In Gander today a modern town has grown up with new schools, churches, supermarkets and all the trappings of progressive, modern life. Every so often one hears a murmur as to what is the future of Gander. This is something that I shall ask the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) to clarify at a later date, but as I see it the future of Gander is secure. It is true that modern, high speed, deluxe transports carry passengers direct from New York to London or Paris or wherever they are going but these represent only a fraction of the growing business of flying.
The great airliners of yesterday are in the tourist trade today. Older planes are carrying freight and the growth of low cost passenger service and air freight is phenomenal. These planes which carry large loads of passengers and freight need to make frequent stops for refueling and all indications are that in the foreseeable future there will be more planes land at Gander instead of fewer and installations at Gander will have to be extended instead of being restricted.
I may say it is particularly gratifying to all Canadians to know that the new terminal at Gander started by the Liberal government will be one of the best in North America. As I stated above, Gander is the only part of Canada which many thousands of people see every year. These people will judge Canada by what they see at Gander. To them Gander is Canada and as Canadians we should be satisfied with nothing but the best at Gander so that we shall advertise ourselves properly. Gander is so important today and, indeed, the Department of Transport has such a heavy interest in Newfoundland that I strongly recommend that it be made a separate region and not be handicapped by being a part of another region and having to do business through Moncton with all the delays which inevitably result from that situation.
Also, Gander badly needs a hotel and the hotel should be built close to the terminal so that passengers arriving fatigued from their trip should not suffer the further exhausting effort of travelling half way around the airport to their quarters. Indeed, they should be able to walk to the hotel.

During the latter part of February and the middle part of March a number of distinguished Canadians visited Newfoundland and gave some attention to the part of Newfoundland which was to become my riding. I fear at the time I did not welcome these attentions with unalloyed pleasure nor was my attitude towards their presence what one would expect from a hospitable Newfoundlander. However, looking back to these visits from the perspective of today I am glad that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the Minister of Transport know at first hand what some of the problems at Gander are, and I can assure them that I will welcome their continued attention to them in the future. If I may, I would solicit across the chasm of political differences the interest in these problems of the minister from Newfoundland.
As I said, one need at Gander is a hotel and the other is a hospital. In this connection I should like to read from an editorial that appeared in the News of December 12, 1957 which, under the heading "Facilities at Gander", had this to say:
So far as we can gather, the Minister of Transport disclaims all responsibility for the removal of the hospital and the provision of new hotel accommodation at Gander. These things, it is said, are not obligations of the department.
In ordinary circumstances, that may be true. But Gander is a special case. It is a Department of Transport town whose whole life is centred around a Department of Transport airport. In the circumstances, responsibility for the provision of essential facilities cannot be easily disclaimed.
Take, for example, the hospital which must hold thirty beds available for the use of the department in any emergency. That itself indicates a direct interest of the transport department in the hospital facilities at Gander.
I may say that the leader of our party pledged the support of our party for financial assistance to the Gander hospital. I would hope the government would come to see the justice of that proposal.
I should like to mention now the desirability of providing television facilities for central Newfoundland. At the present time a microwave line is being built across Newfoundland which will bring live television to St. John's and adjacent areas. This microwave line passes right through central Newfoundland. Certainly, arrangements can be made under which the thickly populated areas of central Newfoundland can be given television service, particularly in view of the fact the microwave lines carrying live television programs pass through this area. It may be that a station built on the height of land between Bishop's Falls and Glenwood might be able to serve an area extending from Buchans in the interior and Lewisporte and vicinity in Notre Dame bay. Included in this
The Address-Mr. Granger area, of course, are such places as Badger, Windsor, Norris Arm, Peter's Arm, Botwood and Point Leamington. However, that is a question for the engineers to settle and if one outlet cannot do the job I think two should be considered. In any event, it is unthinkable to ask an area such as central Newfoundland to do without television facilities in this modern age, particularly when television circuits are passing right through the area. It is like putting a telephone line through a town and denying the inhabitants the use of it.
Mr. Speaker, I have just one or two more subjects to mention before closing, and one has to do with the administration of unemployment insurance for fishermen. Unemployment insurance for fishermen was more than just a boom economically. Its establishment by the Liberal government was the righting of a moral wrong because while the labourers who processed the fish were protected, the men who caught the fish were not. It also did much to preserve the fisheries. The granting of this protection encouraged fishermen to remain at or return to their vocation, and this probably saved it from extinction. However, the actual implementation of unemployment insurance for fishermen has not been too satisfactory. In practically every fishing village I have visited there were many instances of fishermen who qualified for unemployment insurance but were not receiving it. Quite frequently this was the result of misunderstandings, forms not properly filled out, or errors which had to be corrected at the headquarters in Moncton. It is the firm belief of many people that the Department of Labour should employ fieldmen who would travel from place to place assisting fishermen and labourers with their claims and adjusting those miscarriages of justice which too frequently have deprived a producer of getting what was legally his.
It is felt as well that too much time is lost and too much embarrassment is caused by offices in Newfoundland having to refer doubtful claims to remote headquarters. The opinion of the people is that Newfoundland itself should be constituted a region for unemployment insurance purposes. The addition of fieldmen would do much to offset the embarrassing mistakes which are universal.
In concluding, I should like to mention briefly the great northland of which Labrador forms an important part. I am pleased to know the government has in mind the development of the north, and I should like to remind them that Labrador is one of the oldest known and most important parts of Canada's great north. The great iron ore developments, and the water power on the
378	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie Hamilton river as well as the tremendous forests to which so much attention is now being directed, all indicate that Labrador is becoming a princely part of Canada's heritage. I should like to read one or two quotations, and the first is by Lord Strath-cona:
It has been said that power, that empire came from the north. Northern people have always stood for courage and unconquerability They have the muscle, the wholesomeness of life, the strength of will.
The second is from the explorer Stefans-son:
We should not regard the Eskimos as foreigners but as friends. They are your fellow citizens. Their future is bound up in our future. If Canada is but a thin southern strip across which plies a shuttle railway we shall have no remarkable future.
Labrador is indeed a great part of Canada and when we realize its vastness and its untouched riches we begin to appreciate just how young a nation we are in development, and just how great a nation we are becoming. We realize what a greater nation Canada will be in the days of our children's children, when the power and fame of a mature Canada will make an even greater contribution to the material wealth, the peace and goodwill of the brave days of the future.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OP DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I happily conform to tradition, and I do so with all sincerity, in congratulating the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They have followed the high standard which down through the years has been maintained in this parliament. I should like also to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, upon again being chosen as the first commoner. During the throne speech debate of the 23rd parliament I quoted Sir Robert Borden's criterion that a Speaker must be impartial, firm, courteous, and above all patient. I think our Speaker has displayed all those qualities, plus the saving grace of good humour.
I am happy, too, in the choice of a Deputy Speaker because he comes from a distinguished line in the political field. In the 12th parliament his father seconded the address and made such a fine address that the prime minister of that day, Mr. Borden, declared it to be notable and eloquent. His father then went on to occupy the deputy speaker's chair and later the Speaker's chair. It is gratifying to see the hon. member for Spa-dina (Mr. Rea), my friend and counsellor, in the place which he occupies and discharging the duties which he does so well. I might say, in my present congratulatory mood, a word about an hon. member who
[Mr. Granger.)

spoke just a short while ago. I refer to the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Smith). Some time ago he was a student of mine when I walked the halls of learning at Brandon college rather than the legislative halls. I believe, sir, you will agree that if I did nothing else, I made a very good job of training and educating him. We take on a new relationship now. Once I was the professor and he the student. Now, he is the freshman and I am the sophomore.
I was quite interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) yesterday. It seemed to me he divided his time between two roles. At one time he was the politician and at other times he seemed to be the professor. I may say that I preferred him in the professorial role. I would not for a moment suggest that he was a better professor than a politician because it might be a suggestion which could rebound on me some day.
I was interested in his remarks about the development of Canada's political history. I was interested in what he said and I was impressed by the things which he was able to leave unsaid. I was quite surprised that he could speak even as long as he did speak about Canadian autonomy and nationhood without mentioning the name of the great architect of Canadian nationhood, namely Sir Robert Borden. I noted his comment about the mover (Mr. Lafreniere) and the seconder (Mr. Nielsen) of the address and his suggestion that they have the illusion that there were great gaps in Canadian history, that nothing was accomplished during the days when other than a Conservative administration was at the helm. Later on I noted that he spoke of the parable of the 99 out of 100 sheep. As I listened to him I too was reminded of a parable, namely the one about the mote and the beam. I was interested in his nautical metaphors. I followed him through the various passages, which the ship of state took. Perhaps he has reached that stage of nostalgia about which Lowell spoke when he said:
From the days of the first grandfather, everybody has remembered a golden age behind him.
Perhaps the hon. member looks back to the days when he himself was an officer of the ship of state which went through and passed the reefs which he so well recalled yesterday.
I think, however, that it is an extremely healthy sign that members of this house have devoted some time to contemplation of and reflection on Canada's past. It seems to me that it is only recently that many Canadians have awakened to the recognition of the fact that we do indeed have a past in this country. I think it is surely a healthy sign and I have

been greatly interested in the comments which have been made in this throne speech debate. On occasion I expected to hear more about a certain recent date in the past, namely the date of March 31. On occasion some comments were made about it but often it was passed over. On reflection, I think it is perhaps just as well. The verdict has been given. I think the members of the winning party are to be congratulated. The fact that they have restrained completely any tendency to gloat over or to boast about what has been done and what has taken place on the electoral level is to be commended. There has been no castigating and no crying "Aha" over what has happened. Macaulay once pointed to Peel in the British house and said:
There you sit doing penance for the disingenuousness of years.
That accusation, of course, could never be made against the party which once sat on the treasury benches of this country.
In reflecting upon the election, I find myself in disagreement with the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I do not think that this past election could be described as a Madison Avenue election. I am rather inclined to think that it is one of the most serious elections which this country has held. I think it has given on the part of the Canadian people a display of intelligent calculation and analysis that is quite unique. I do not say that while projecting my thoughts along to the result. I think there was a particular reason why this election was a serious exercise of intelligence on the part of the Canadian people. The reason was that it was a quite unique experience.
On March 31 the voters of Canada had the opportunity to compare and to contrast two known alternatives. No voter was so young that he could not recall vividly what had been done and what had not been done by the Liberal party in its many years in office. Hence there was no necessity for appraising new panaceas, platforms and programs. The mere exercise of memory was sufficient. The judgment was made and of course we know the result.
I also think that there is developing on the parliamentary scene a seriousness of purpose and a realization of the responsibilities that go with power. This is reflected in the speech from the throne; and of all that document contains, the most important and the most imperishable will be those things which reveal the government's determination to avoid that unhappy state when power turns to tyranny and authority becomes arrogance. I think the Canadian people can be thankful that such determination is there and will be maintained. In days past we can remember that
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie such was not the case. I had an experience similar to that recalled by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George the other day, when we observed the use and the abuse of power in this Canadian parliament. I am sure that we all agree, regardless of our party label, that such should never occur again in this country.
It is a stimulating experience to hear the speeches of hon. members from all parts of this country. I have listened with great interest to the hon. members as they described the glories and virtues of their constituencies. Of course, it is easy to paint such pictures about a great and growing country like Canada. This nation has before it a wonderful future, marked by progress and prosperity within its borders and an increasing importance and significance in the affairs of the world. But the healthy economic development of Canada requires a degree of prosperity in all parts of the country. It is in the national interest to assure that no region in the country falls noticeably below the over-all level of prosperity.
It is possible that one may now anticipate one of these ancient instruments of Canadian politics, namely a speech on maritime rights, that substance on which all maritime politicians are weaned and nurtured. As Canada's history has progressed, the maritime provinces have fallen behind. Sometimes we maritimers-and we are sentimental people at all times-are accused of reminiscing too much about the good old days. Sometimes it is said that a maritimer talks about confederation as if it were an event that had taken place the day before yesterday. But our area once had great prosperity. While perhaps it is easy to confuse coincidence with cause, it is nevertheless true that in economic terms there has been a decline since the time of confederation. This is a theme of great interest to us all.
But I happen to represent the province in which confederation was born. In that great city which is in the riding which I represent along with my senior colleague, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean), namely the city of Charlottetown, confederation was born in 1864. But during the years after that great ideal was put into actuality, confederation seemed to move westward from the land of its birth: "westward the course of empire ever stayed". The hinterland of the old Canadian provinces was opened up. Then the march across the prairies began under the distinguished and inspired leadership of the founder of the Conservative party and its great exten-tion was magnificent for Canada, but the gulf between the rest of Canada and the maritimes widened.

The Address-Mr. Macquarrie
The concentration of wealth and population in the central provinces, adverse tariff policies, inadequate and costly transportation, have added to the burdens and increased the disparity. There resulted a further relative depression in the maritime provinces. Our people-among the finest in the land-found it necessary to leave for other parts of Canada and for the United States. Statistics are never popular, but there is one which is so significant that I must ask the forbearance of this house in order to quote it. In the year 1881 the population of Prince Eward Island was 108,900 people. At the same time the population of British Columbia was 49,459. Today our population has suffered an actual decline and there are less than 100,000 people in my province, while in British Columbia there are well over 1,000,000 people. In that simple statistic there is a revelation.
During the years that have passed the people of the maritime area have asked the question: "Are the maritime provinces to become a permanently depressed area; are they only to be a quaint and picturesque community with hospitable and charming people, so well beloved of the tourist, but to lose their rightful place in the modern economic life of Canada?" There was a danger that along with the economic depression there might develop something far more serious-a mental depression among the people of the area.
Happily our outlook is better today. There is a new spirit abroad in the old provinces by the sea. A new feeling of hope, a new sense of purpose and direction are abroad. As the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stewart) mentioned a while ago, this is evidenced by the thinking which found expression at the Atlantic provinces' economic council and was further revealed in the Atlantic premiers' conference. The vigour and vision of these two great maritime leaders, Premier Stanfield and Premier Flemming, have served as a source of stimulation and challenge to all of us. It has been said many times that the administrative costs of four separate governments are very high in the maritimes and indeed have been called simply ridiculous, but there is no possibility of the four little provinces in the Atlantic region cheerfully yielding their identity. They will remain provinces and they will remain distinct, but while they retain their identity there is no reason why they cannot further their co-operative efforts and it is in that spirit that the new developments in the maritimes are progressing.
We all welcome the admission of a new neighbour, Newfoundland. We in Prince Edward Island were particularly happy


because we have surplus of the finest agricultural products and we welcome Newfoundland because there is no one we would more like to have purchase our products. I believe that provincial governments and other groups should stimulate trade between Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland, and I am thoroughly convinced that the possibilities have not been sufficiently tapped or developed.
While self-help is important and this is being developed, the assistance and the initiative of the central government is essential. Herein lies the explanation of both the economic and the political changes in the maritime area in recent months. As I have said, confederation was born in my province but through the years the centre of gravity has moved westward, leaving the maritimes in the periphery of prosperity. How interesting it is that at this historic stage in our development out of the west should come a national leader who saw the vision and took the steps to redress that balance which had left us to one side.
I say the steps he took were in the national interest. Canada is immeasurably stronger today in every way as the result of what this government did in its first few months in office. The Atlantic provinces' adjustment acts, the Beechwood project, the aid to thermal power development and the rest, these brought new hope to our area. Prince Edward Island gained a grant of $2J million. We are very simple and unsophisticated people down there, and none of us will ever say, "What's a million?" What that million meant to us was one-quarter of our total budget and it was the largest single grant which ever came to our province from the federal treasury.
I would like to say that nothing will ever give me a greater sense of pride than to have belonged to the parliament, in a very humble capacity, which in a short time did so much for my province and the Atlantic provinces in general, who have for so long cried out and received not the answer they sought.
This explains why the maritime provinces gave their support wholeheartedly and unreservedly to the man who had sufficient breadth of vision to realize that in the interests of all of Canada this long-neglected region must be given immediate, urgent and ample attention and, if I may be a bit immodest, I cannot help mentioning that my province led the way and that in the election of June 10 Prince Edward Island formed a 100 per cent club of supporters of the Diefen-baker government. We were very happy that our neighbour Nova Scotia, that Alberta and Manitoba also joined this club, but we claim the right to reserve the title charter member.

I would not be a true maritimer, nor would I be a good representative of the historic constituency of Queens if I left the impression with you, Mr. Speaker, or with this chamber or with the government that our needs had all been met and that in the maritimes milk and honey flow gushingly. There have been many remarks about the fishing industry, the second industry in the province of Prince Edward Island. We feel confident about the future of the fishing industry because my long-time friend and colleague, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. MacLean) is assuming responsibility for that important part of our economy. In Prince Edward Island, however, and in the maritimes generally, the question of transportation is of the utmost importance. We must have better transportation facilities so that the products of our farms and the sea may be moved more expeditiously to the markets we have developed.
Down through the years the men who have preceded me have called the attention of the house and of the government to the inadequacy of the transportation between our island province and the rest of Canada.
When Prince Edward Island joined confederation in 1873, part of the understanding was that continous communication should be maintained between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island. As the hon. member for Westmorland (Mr. Creaghan) pointed out the other day, we do not at the present time have adequate transportation, and the people of my province rejoice that again in this respect the new government moved rapidly. There is going on today an exhaustive survey of the possibility, in all its aspects, of building the causeway which has been projected between Borden, Prince Edward Island, and Cape Jourmain in New Brunswick. We look forward to the day when history will repeat itself and when a Conservative government will establish the most up-to-date transportation link between our historic province and the rest of Canada. It was the government of Sir Robert Borden which gave us our first car ferry, and we look forward to the time when another Conservative government will make possible this causeway
The Address-Mr. Macquarrie
which, some of my more chauvinistic followers would say, will join Canada to Prince Edward Island.
We feel there are sound reasons for this work going forward. Not only would it facilitate the movement of tourists, but it would simplify the movement of our goods. Prince Edward Island is a mecca for tourists, one of those places to which people return again and again. We want to make these visits easier and we also want to facilitate the movement of goods from our farms. Prince Edward Island is sometimes described as the garden of the gulf. We are blessed with a fertile soil, and the products of our soil command top prices on the commodity markets.
There are many items which I could discuss in my present expansive mood, but I do not wish to place too many of the problems of our area before the government at one time. In Prince Edward Island we have one basic problem-the potato. We in this House are still greatly concerned about an industry which was once the leading industry in Canada-agriculture. We are taking a great interest in what has been done for the prairie farmers. What has been done for those farmers deserves to be done. We, in Prince Edward Island and in the east, rejoiced in the legislation providing cash advances on farm-stored grain; we were interested in the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act and in the assistance given in the matter of freight rates. But we in Prince Edward Island produce another commodity which is our most vital commodity, namely the potato. We feel that producers of the potato should not be in any more precarious a position than are growers of wheat in another part of Canada. Throughout the years the potato industry has been marked by great uncertainty and wide fluctuations in price. At one point a farmer may get $2.50 a bushel; shortly afterwards he may find it impossible to get more than 50 cents. We call upon the government to take advantage of the Agricultural Prices Stabilization Act to stabilize in the best and most practical manner the price of this vital commodity. The potato is not among the named commodities mentioned in the act, but at the present time we face a situation which calls for action, and on behalf of the agriculturists in my province I ask that thorough consideration be given to providing stability and security for these very important producers.
Mr. Speaker, one always tries to live up to the characteristics of the region from which one comes, and one of the characteristics of our people is brevity. I should be very much

It is quite true that Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir George Etienne Cartier deserve a special place in Canadian history as fathers of our nation but it is equally true that other great prime ministers have played a useful, brilliant and extremely important part in the building up of Canada. Sir Wilfrid Laurier, perhaps the greatest of them all, William Lyon Mackenzie King and Louis St. Laurent have been successful contributors to the achievement of the aims that have been those of all Canadians who want to live in a country free from fear, disunity, economic hardship and unemployment; the aims of all Canadians who want to live in a country enjoying the complete status of a free and independent nation without at the same time having to sever its intimate cultural and economic links with our mother countries.
As to the Prime Minister, the future alone will identify the place he will hold in our history. Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with the most pressing problem now facing parliament, that of unemployment. In spite of the optimistic statements of certain government members-and in this connection I refer more particularly to that made by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) who stated in Hamilton on April 21 last:
. . . that those elements which have brought about a levelling of economic activity in Canada are, generally speaking, of a temporary nature and for the most part originated outside our own borders; that unemployment is not so much due to an economic recession as to an abnormally high increase in the working force; that the workers' income has increased by 7 per cent, personal income by 6 per cent and, finally, that export trade has reached an unprecedentedly high level.
In spite of such optimistic statements, in spite of a small decrease in unemployment announced in yesterday's newspapers, to be realistic is the course of wisdom. Unemployment exists to an extremely critical degree.
At the end of April, Canadian newspapers reported that one out of ten employables was unemployed. Today, more than 800,000 people are registered with the National Employment Office as seeking work. This is the largest total on record since the inception of this service.
Considering that since the last months of 1957 the number of unemployed has increased at the rate of more than 20,000 per month, we cannot help but feel that the situation will become really alarming.
Did not Mr. C. A. L. Murchison, unemployment insurance commissioner, state in Montreal at the beginning of this month that the Unemployment Insurance Commission fund was threatened with depletion in less than six years, if the present rate of contributions and benefits is maintained. During the fiscal year ended on March 31st last, the Commission has paid out, in unemployment benefits, a higher amount than was paid out during its first 11 years of existence (1940-1951), that is over $385 million.
The hardships caused by unemployment are not, however, so disastrously felt as during
The Address-Mr. Eudes the last depression. Each month, unemployment benefits, old age pensions, family allowances, and benefits of all kinds which, as a result of the social legislation introduced by the previous governments, have put money into the pocketbook of the consumers are a powerful remedy to the hardships which otherwise would inevitably come with unemployment.
However, those social measures, as well as the amendment passed last week to the unemployment insurance act, are only stop-gaps. They do not reach the root of the unemployment problem, and cannot solve it in any way whatsoever.
Moreover, at some definite date, the right to those unemployment insurance benefits will come to an end for every unemployed.
What truly earnest effort, fairly likely to succeed, has the government made to stop or alleviate the swell of unemployment?
Yet, the rate of unemployment is alarming at least since October last. To be convinced, one has simply to refer to the speeches delivered in this house since the opening of this parliament and in particular to the speech made by the hon. member for Resti-gouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne). This unemployment is the most serious economic upheaval that can happen to a country.
Is there a more distressing spectacle than that of a human being, who by nature and God's will was placed on earth to work and who, without being in the least responsible for it, suddenly finds himself unemployed.
As the leader of the opposition has said, a man out of work is not a statistic but a challenge to society. He is evidently unable to play his essential role in the mechanism of society, that of contributing to civilization by his work, however humble, and of supplying his family with food, clothing, shelter and that strict minimum without which no human being can make a fruitful use of his talents. Work is to the city what fecundity is to the family. Every employable human being must be a productive cog.
Yet there is unemployment and, at the domestic policy level, the federal government is thus charged with an imperative, serious and unescapable responsibility. Before anything else, it must become aware of the existence of this extremely painful problem, then study it and finally prescribe efficient remedies.
It would be ridiculous to attempt to share this responsibility, which rests squarely on
384	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Eudes the central government, with the governments of ten provinces and innumerable municipalities, because of our constitutional system, of particular conditions affecting our economy, such as the need for export trade, of the nature of our production, of the fact that a relatively small population is widely scattered over a huge territory.
But is not that the opinion of the Prime Minister himself? Is that not what we may conclude from his statements before the last parliament and especially during the last election campaign? Did he not proclaim that if the country were to elect him with a sufficiently stable majority, he would solve this unemployment problem immediately? That majority he now has, possibly beyond his wildest dreams.
And now, Mr. Speaker, we are waiting and waiting anxiously for this promise to be fulfilled in order that our country may recover the economic balance it has lost since June 10, 1957.
The solution to this alarming problem of unemploynent therefore rests squarely on the shoulders of the federal government. It would be unreasonable not only to believe but even to imagine that the governments of ten provinces, that municipal councils, in our cities and towns and rural areas, are capable in the least of influencing those factors which affect our national economy, those innumerable factors which are the immediate or remote superficial or deep causes of this preposterous situation. How is it that in a country as prosperous as ours, as well endowed with every kind of possibility, 10 per cent at least of our workers now find themselves without a job?
Of course, if it were possible to determine with mathematical precision the basic cause of unemployment, the problem would be much easier to solve.
However, the causes are numerous and interrelated to such a point that it is practically impossible to say with certainty which is the most important, the one which has set the others into play.
Economists agree, and rightly so, that the immediate cause of unemployment is the excessive unsold inventories intended for the domestic market, or for export markets which are considered as absolutely necessary and as a constant prerequisite to our economic balance . . .

Indeed our farmers, our fishermen, our manufacturers are producing much more than we can consume here in Canada. Now when this failure to sell our products reaches a certain level it causes an economic disorder: overproduction.
I use the word disorder purposely because overproduction is a sign of disorder, disorder in the minds of producers who, in their estimations, too often forget the essential action of the law of supply and demand, disorder too in the minds of men who having sought, obtained and accepted the difficult task of managing the affairs of the country should now channel our production so that it may find outlets on the domestic market as well as on foreign markets.
Is there no disorder when there is overproduction?
Let us think for a moment of the needs of those millions of people scattered over the world who lack the essential things for their immediate requirements, let us think of this being called man, perhaps a Canadian, whose needs are not only unfulfilled but far from adequate.
This overproduction and this sales slump of our products are necessarily due to lack of purchasing power both at home and abroad.
But then what is, in turn, the cause of this lack of purchasing power? The causes are manifold: first, unsound production programs, based not so much on the needs and desires of the consumer than on the producer's stubborn idea of forcing the public to buy through middlemen and advertising, thus involving expenses that double the actual cost price. Unsound commercial policy, neglecting external markets that might be excellent outlets for the disposal of our products while favouring others, often from sentimental reasons, that actually bring us only rather embarrassing customers. Unsound programs

in the matter of credit which, in some fields is excessive, with attendant dangers of growing inflation, while in other cases it is restricted to the point of paralysing industries which otherwise could activate an easily marketable production and create jobs for thousands of workers.
There are evidently other causes for lack of buying power, which it would be useless to discuss at this time, because they are only corollaries of those already mentioned.
Now production, foreign and domestic markets, credit, buying power and overproduction, all these aspects come under federal jurisdiction.
This government intends to embark on a public works policy in order to check unemployment. Without rejecting this suggestion, I do not believe that such public expenses which, after all, are carried by the taxpayer, will bring about the immediate alleviation of unemployment which it demands. The very planning and preparation of such projects call for a period of several months. They may also make necessary a migration of people who, when the project has been completed, will again be unemployed if other local industries are unable to absorb this labour force when it becomes available.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, that serious consideration should be given to the buying power of the consumer and to his needs, on the domestic as well as on the foreign market. I also believe that producers should be guided by results thus obtained, as to the nature, the volume and the distribution of their production; and that foreign trade should be directed to the countries needing our goods or which, in their turn, are able to sell us the essential commodities we lack.
Those principles are extremely simple but nevertheless hold the key to the unemployment problem.
To those considerations may be added some practical suggestions, for instance the development of small industries, giving the economy a greater individual flexibility by maintaining a class of craftsmen assured of their living, as the fate of the working classes often depends upon the destiny of a single day; care that credit does not unduly sustain the production of articles that might not sell, or that credit does not pave the way for another frightful evil, inflation.
In order to increase at once the purchasing power, several steps come to mind, such as: (a) immediate tax exemption at all levels, which is less liable to produce inflation than public expenditures and which, through the
The Address-Mr. Bourbonnais resumption of business, will in no way affect the treasury, since it will bring about an increase in tax collection at the lower levels, which will offset any losses incurred at the higher levels; (b) extend family allowances until age 18 for students; (c) grant unemployment insurance benefits to those who must quit their work because of illness; (d) grant the old age assistance benefits to widows and spinsters as soon as they reach the age of 60.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the problem of unemployment is, by its very nature, the most alarming problem a government has to deal with in domestic affairs; this is a problem which bears upon its conscience, whether it likes it or not.
The right hon. Prime Minister promised to solve this problem if the people would give him their confidence. He now has this confidence, as well as all available means to put an end to this distressing situation which, in our country, after 22 years of prosperity, of security which we have known under the governments of Mr. Mackenzie King and Mr. St. Laurent, is a challenge to democracy and to mankind.

Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the population of Vaudreuil-Soulanges riding which I represent, 1 wish to offer you my most sincere congratulations upon your election to the high office you now hold. I wish to offer the same mark of respect to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fair-clough); the Minister of Defence Production (Mr. O'Hurley); the Secretary of State (Mr. Courtemanche) for their appointments to cabinet posts. I should like also to join with other members in extending congratulations to the Deputy Speaker, the hon. member for Longueuil (Mr. Sevigny). May I add my words of appreciation to those of other hon. members for the wonderful address moved by the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Lafreniere), seconded by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen).
I should like to express to this house the gratitude I owe to the people of my county for the confidence they have put in me, and may God help me to represent them with respect and dignity. The riding of Vaudreuil-Soulanges has four times elected your predecessor in the chair, Mr. Speaker. I want to ask the whole house to be lenient and not judge him too harshly in the light of the

The Aadress-Mr. Bourbonnais news which appeared in yesterday's newspapers. In all fairness to the people I represent, I must say that the hon. Mr. Beaudoin was not born, brought up or educated in Vaudreuil-Soulanges. My county has elected such well-known politicians as Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Senator Boyer and Senator Wilson.
I am very proud to say that these members were amongst the best of the Liberals who represented Vaudreuil-Soulanges almost exclusively since confederation.
Vaudreuil-Soulanges is typical of the province of Quebec. It is situated at the doorstep of Montreal, bordered by the province of Ontario on the west, on the north by the Ottawa river and on the south by the St. Lawrence river. It is crisscrossed by our two major railroads, the Canadian National railways and the Canadian Pacific railway. It is also the fork of the Montreal, Ottawa and Toronto highways. It is typical of the whole province of Quebec, being populated by approximately one-third of English speaking Canadians and two-thirds of French speaking Canadians and the best of relations are maintained between the two groups.
It it also typical of the province of Quebec because it reacts in the same way as the majority of Quebec. Our main occupation is farming and dairying. A great number of our people earn their living as tradesmen. They have to commute to Montreal from the suburbs to earn their living. A good many of them are office workers. We have few industries inside the county to help our people to earn their living. The Soulanges canal is our most beautiful landmark and one of our major industries, it will cease its operations when the St. Lawrence seaway is open to navigation next summer. The men working on the canal will eventually be laid off, thus increasing the number of those unemployed which is quite impressive as of now. I have confidence in the future; I have confidence that the future will brighten for us because the Conservatives are in power now.
Here, Mr. Speaker, I want to refer back to history. The Soulanges canal was built some 65 years ago by a Conservative government and it brought to my county work and progress. The decision to close it was taken under a Liberal administration and it brought sorrows and worries to very many people. Now that the Conservatives are back in power we have confidence in the future and my election is a proof of the confidence of the people in the Conservative party.
Another question that I have very much at heart is the development of our municipalities in Vaudreuil-Soulanges, in the province of Quebec as well as in the whole

of Canada. I refer to development of our municipalities without breaking the bank account of all our proprietors. I must say that municipal affairs are under provincial jurisdicition, and for that matter they are well taken care of by our provincial government. But in Quebec after 40 years of Liberal administration the actual government of Quebec had to build everything. It had to build new schools at the rate of one a day. It is still doing so and it can hardly keep up with the need. It had to build hospitals by the dozens. It had to spend billions for roads and bridges. It had to take countless measures to help the poor farmers of our province who were left penniless after the depression. It had to spend all kinds of money to help them live. It had to bring the province of Quebec to the level of the other provinces of Canada. For that reason I shall always have admiration and great respect for the premier of the province of Quebec, regardless of all criticism against him from whatever source it may come.
To come back to the subject of our municipalities I want to mention the state of our small towns and villages that seem to belong to the last century more than to this atomic age. Most of them need water systems, sewerage systems, roads, firefighting equipment, playgrounds and so on but they cannot undertake any project of that kind because of the high cost due in part to the high rate of interest charged on loans and the low price paid for their municipal bonds. It so happens that when a municipal corporation has paid up a debt for a project it has paid approximately twice the amount of the original cost. It is very discouraging for the taxpayers.
Since the federal government has found a way to finance construction of private homes, could it not find a way in which to help finance at a fraction of the current interest rate all municipal corporation public projects? I am sure if such a scheme could be worked out a great number of municipal projects now sleeping in as many city halls would be undertaken and started fairly soon. It would also give work to very many as well as activate slowed-down industries.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my thanks to the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) for so kindly having lent his personality during the last campaign; also to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming), the Solicitor General (Mr. Balcer) and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Hees) for their visit to my county which meant victory for me. May I add my thanks also to the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) for some wise words as reported

in Time of February 17, 1958, at page 14, which are as follows:
It would be foolish and unfair to try to pin unemployment on the Conservatives.
Those words balanced marvelously some too Liberal publicity directed against us. It would not be fair not to include some thanks to the Toronto Daily Star for the free publicity it gave me during the campaign. Imagine my picture being next to the Prime Minister on the front page of that paper. Now that the Tories have finally wiped out all prejudice between Toronto and Quebec, it is very hard for a Quebecker awaiting the hockey season to leave Toronto alone altogether.

In the Gatineau district the tourist industry ranks second in importance in the constituency. Thousands of tourists come there each year to spend their vacation, either to rest and admire the natural beauty of our lakes, forests and mountains, or for fishing or hunting. Vacationing attracts thousands of tourists, especially American tourists because part of the constituency is located in the area of the national capital, about 60 miles from the border of the most populous state of the United States, the state of New York.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to conclude these remarks by putting forward a suggestion for the government's consideration. This would be a long term project for the

The Address-Mr. Leduc good of my constituency and of the Ottawa-Hull area as well as, generally speaking, for the residents of both banks of the river. This suggestion I put to the government because it claimed before the last elections and during the campaign itself that it was unable to undertake long term projects because it did not have a stable majority in the house.
Well, the government has that majority now and I put forward that suggestion which I consider feasible after having studied it with competent engineers. This could be carried out jointly by the Ottawa government, the Quebec and Ontario governments and the municipalities concerned. I refer here to the construction of a pipe line for the transportation of pure water from 31 Mile lake through the villages and the valley of the Gatineau river to serve the whole Hull area and the whole of the Ottawa valley so as to provide the people there with a pure water supply. Water would run down the Gatineau mountainsides by force of gravity, there being a difference of altitude of more than 350 feet between Ottawa and the 31 Mile lake. Consequently, this pipe-line would eliminate filtration plants, pumping units and chlorination plants. That, in my opinion, is the logical solution to the problem of pure water supply for the whole Gatineau area and the Ottawa valley.
Cities like New York bring in drinking water over hundreds of miles from distant lakes to supply their needs, and the city of Syracuse brings in the water it requires through a pipe-line from lake Skaneateles over a distance of 15 miles. This project would cost perhaps 30 million dollars or more, but it would pay for itself and it is the duty of the governments concerned to study the matter and find once and for all the solution to the problem of supplying the whole Ottawa area with pure drinking water.
Mr. Speaker, you are no doubt aware that the city of Ottawa is the only city in this area having a water filtration plant on the Ottawa river. Indeed, Ottawa papers reported yesterday that a new filtration plant would be built in Britannia at a cost of $5 million. Not all cities and municipalities of the Ottawa area have filtration plants. They have to supply water to residents of the area. The Ottawa river is recognized as an open sewer and there are no purification plants for all the sewerage being poured into the Ottawa river. Going down from Aylmer and Britannia, the Ottawa river is polluted as far as Montreal and residents on both shores of the river have to drink that water after a strong chlorine solution has been added to it.
Well, in my opinion, as a means of reducing unemployment and of helping the municipali-

I consider that such a project would promote the welfare, the development and the progress of that area.
